components.name: The Sazerac
components.explain:
The Sazerac is New Orleans' own cocktail: rye whiskey, sugar and Peychaud's bitters, stirred cold and strained into a glass rinsed with an anise spirit, served without ice.

Its name comes from a cognac. Sewell Taylor sold his bar, the Merchants Exchange Coffee House, to import Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, and Aaron Bird renamed the bar the Sazerac Coffee House and served the house cocktail on that cognac. Thomas Handy took the bar over about 1870, just as phylloxera was ruining the vineyards of Europe, and rye whiskey took the cognac's place for good.

On 23 June 2008 the Louisiana Legislature made it the official cocktail of the city of New Orleans, not of the state. At Brennan's it is a ladder of three: the Classic, Thompson's Dream and the Origin Story.

card.front: Why is the Sazerac named Sazerac?
card.back: It was the house drink of the Sazerac Coffee House, named for Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac. Rye replaced the cognac after phylloxera; since 2008 it is New Orleans' official cocktail.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Antoine Peychaud, the apothecary on Royal Street
components.explain:
Antoine Amédée Peychaud was a Creole apothecary born in Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, who settled in New Orleans. He kept his shop at what was then 123 Royal Street, known as 437 Royal Street today, on the same block as Brennan's at 417.

There he made a bright red aromatic bitters, sold first as a tonic, between 1849 and 1857. In 1857 he advertised his American Aromatic Bitter Cordial and announced it was in use at the Sazerac House. He sold the Royal Street building in 1868, and the bitters passed through other hands to the Sazerac Company.

A guest may tell you Peychaud invented the word cocktail from a French egg cup. Smile: the word was defined in print in 1806. Tell the true story instead, and check at lineup that the house is happy for the Royal Street detail to be told.

card.front: Where did Antoine Peychaud keep his apothecary?
card.back: At what is now 437 Royal Street, the same block as Brennan's at 417. He made his red bitters there in the 1850s and they went into the first Sazeracs.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p39, the Classic Sazerac service note)

components.name: The word cocktail, 1806
components.explain:
The first printed definition of a cocktail appeared on 13 May 1806 in The Balance and Columbian Repository, a newspaper in Hudson, New York. Its editor, Harry Croswell, answered a reader: a cocktail is a stimulating liquor of spirits of any kind, sugar, water and bitters.

That four-part formula is the Old Fashioned, and it is the skeleton of the Sazerac and of the Champagne Cocktail, where Champagne stands in for the spirit and the water at once.

The story matters because guests love the tale that Antoine Peychaud coined the word from the French egg cup, the coquetier. He was a small child in 1806, so the tale cannot be true. Never call the Sazerac America's first cocktail; call it New Orleans' official cocktail, which is true and sells better.

card.front: What four things made a cocktail in the 1806 definition?
card.back: Spirits of any kind, sugar, water and bitters, printed in May 1806. It is the Old Fashioned pattern, the skeleton of the Sazerac, the Birdcage and the Champagne Cocktail.

components.name: Absinthe, banned and back
components.explain:
Absinthe is a strong spirit distilled with grand wormwood, green anise and fennel, usually bottled between 55 and 70 percent alcohol and traditionally louched, slowly diluted with cold water until it turns cloudy.

In 1912 the United States Department of Agriculture banned it, treating wormwood drinks as adulterated. New Orleans, which had loved absinthe through the nineteenth century, turned to substitutes, Herbsaint above all. On 5 March 2007 the federal authorities confirmed that wormwood spirits could be sold again if they were thujone free, and American and French absinthes returned to the bars.

At Brennan's this is why the ladder changes its rinse: the Classic uses Herbsaint, the substitute born of the ban, while Thompson's Dream uses St. George, the first American absinthe after 2007, and the Origin Story uses Jade Nouvelle-Orléans.

card.front: When was absinthe banned in the United States, and when did it return?
card.back: Banned in 1912 and legal again in 2007, if thujone free. Herbsaint was created in the gap; our premium Sazeracs use real absinthe rinses.

components.name: Why it is called the Origin Story
components.explain:
The Origin Story is the top of the house's Sazerac ladder, and its name points back to how the drink began. The first Sazeracs were poured at the Sazerac Coffee House on Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac with Antoine Peychaud's bitters.

Phylloxera, a root-eating insect, reached the vineyards of Cognac in the 1870s and made cognac scarce through the 1880s; rye whiskey took over and never gave the drink back. So a Sazerac on cognac is the drink as it started.

Say it carefully: the way it began, cognac and Peychaud's, rather than the exact first recipe, because the absinthe rinse probably joined later. Offer it to the guest who has had the Classic and wants to taste where it came from, or at the Chateaubriand table.

card.front: Why is the Origin Story built on cognac?
card.back: The first Sazeracs were cognac and Peychaud's; rye replaced cognac after phylloxera ruined the vineyards. The Origin Story returns to the way the drink began.

components.name: The name Thompson's Dream
components.explain:
Thompson's Dream is the middle rung of the Sazerac ladder, built on Willett 4-year rye. The name is the house's own: no Willett bottling carries it.

The Willett Distilling Company was founded in 1936 on the family farm in Bardstown, Kentucky, with Thompson Willett as its founder and president and his brother Johnny beside him. The first whiskey ran on 17 March 1937. The old distillery closed in the 1980s and the family began distilling on the site again in 2012.

So a server says the name is probably a nod to Thompson Willett, the distillery's founder, and never says it as settled fact. If a guest wants more, it is a fine question to bring back from the bar or a manager.

card.front: Who is Thompson's Dream probably named for?
card.back: Probably Thompson Willett, who founded the Willett distillery in Bardstown in 1936. No Willett bottle carries the name, so say probably, never certainly.

components.name: Milk punch
components.explain:
Milk punch is one of the oldest mixed drinks in the English-speaking world, and it comes in two families. The old English kind is clarified: hot milk is added to spirit, citrus and sugar, the milk curdles, and the curds are strained out, leaving a clear, silky punch that keeps. Mary Rockett wrote one down in 1711, and Benjamin Franklin wrote out his own recipe in 1763.

The New Orleans kind is the other family: brandy or bourbon with milk or cream, sugar and vanilla, shaken cold and dusted with nutmeg, never clarified.

Brennan's pours both ideas. The Brandy Milk Punch is the cold, creamy eye opener that opens the Traditional Breakfast; the Prisoner of Love on the fall list uses clarified heavy cream, the old English technique.

card.front: What are the two kinds of milk punch?
card.back: The old clarified kind, curdled and strained clear, as in the Prisoner of Love; and the cold, creamy New Orleans kind, our Brandy Milk Punch, shaken with cream and nutmeg.

components.name: The eye opener
components.explain:
In New Orleans a proper late breakfast starts with an eye opener: a morning cocktail poured before the food. The menu groups four of them as the classic eye openers: the Brandy Milk Punch, the Bloody Bull, Brennan's Bloody Mary and Brennan's Irish Coffee.

The habit belongs to the city's long, leisurely breakfasts, the kind Brennan's made famous, where a meal of several courses runs from the milk punch to the Bananas Foster.

For a server it is a selling rhythm. Offer the milk punch at the greeting, before menus open: it is the first sale of the morning and course one of the Traditional Breakfast. The Bloody Bull follows with the soup course. A guest not drinking is offered the Café Glacé de la Maison or the Revive juice instead, so nobody misses the ritual.

card.front: Name Brennan's four classic eye openers.
card.back: The Brandy Milk Punch, the Bloody Bull, Brennan's Bloody Mary and Brennan's Irish Coffee. Offer the milk punch at the greeting: it is the first sale of the morning.

components.name: The Bloody Mary and the Bull Shot
components.explain:
The Bloody Mary is often credited to Fernand Petiot, a bartender at Harry's New York Bar in Paris about 1921, where it began as vodka and tomato juice. In 1934 he took it to the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis in New York and seasoned it with Worcestershire, lemon, salt, pepper and Tabasco; the hotel tried to call it the Red Snapper. Other claimants exist, so say credited.

The Bull Shot came from the Caucus Club in Detroit in 1952: vodka with cold canned beef bouillon, dreamed up to sell more bouillon.

A Bloody Bull is the two together, tomato and beef. The guide calls ours a Brennan's breakfast classic; it never says it was invented here, and neither should a server.

card.front: What is a Bloody Bull, in family terms?
card.back: A Bloody Mary crossed with a Bull Shot: tomato mix, vodka and beef bouillon. Call it a Brennan's breakfast classic, never an invention of the house.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Irish coffee
components.explain:
Irish coffee was born at Foynes, the flying boat terminal in County Limerick, in 1943. When a flight turned back in bad weather, the chef, Joe Sheridan, warmed the passengers with coffee laced with Irish whiskey, sugar and cream; asked if it was Brazilian coffee, he said no, Irish coffee.

On 10 November 1952 Jack Koeppler of the Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco and the travel writer Stanton Delaplane set out to recreate it, and Sheridan later moved to San Francisco to work there.

The rules have not changed: a warmed glass, sugar dissolved in hot coffee, the whiskey, then cream floated on top and never stirred. Brennan's adds a New Orleans accent with chicory coffee and brown sugar, and pours it at breakfast and with dessert.

card.front: Where and when was Irish coffee first served?
card.back: At Foynes, the flying boat terminal in County Limerick, in 1943, by the chef Joe Sheridan. It reached San Francisco's Buena Vista Cafe in 1952.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: The espresso martini
components.explain:
The espresso martini is a London drink of the 1980s. It is credited to the bartender Dick Bradsell, often dated to 1983 at the Soho Brasserie, who mixed vodka, fresh espresso, coffee liqueur and sugar for a guest who wanted something to wake her up. It was first called the Vodka Espresso; the martini name came later with the cocktail glass.

A hard shake is what makes it: the coffee's oils whip into a fine tan foam that sits on top.

Ours is a New Orleans version. The menu prints chicory, vodka, Frangelico and Kahlua, so it carries the city's chicory and a hazelnut note, and the menu does not print espresso. How the coffee goes in is a question for the bar before a server describes it.

card.front: Who is credited with the espresso martini, and where?
card.back: The London bartender Dick Bradsell, in the 1980s, often dated 1983 at the Soho Brasserie. Ours adds chicory and Frangelico; the menu does not print espresso.

components.name: The Champagne Cocktail
components.explain:
The Champagne Cocktail is one of the oldest named drinks with wine. Jerry Thomas printed it in his bar guide of 1862: a lump of sugar soaked in Angostura bitters in a wine glass, filled with Champagne, finished with lemon peel. Nobody knows who first made it.

It is the 1806 cocktail formula in sparkling form: the Champagne is spirit and water at once, the cube is the sugar and the bitters soak it. As the cube dissolves it keeps throwing a thin stream of bubbles up through the glass.

At Brennan's it is the house's bubbly classic, priced at the top of the Bubbles cocktails. Which Champagne, the glass and any garnish are confirmed with the bar; the build on the menu is the classic one.

card.front: Who first printed the Champagne Cocktail, and when?
card.back: Jerry Thomas, in his bar guide of 1862: a sugar cube soaked in Angostura, topped with Champagne and lemon peel. Ours prints a demerara cube.

components.name: Bubbles at Brennan's
components.explain:
Bubbles at Brennan's is the house's afternoon Champagne service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, Monday to Friday from 2 to 6, with Champagne sabred on Fridays at 5, as the guide prints.

Its menu carries five bubbly cocktails, rosé bottles and bar snacks. The Riviera, the Bodrum and the OBX sit at the friendly price, the Chandon Garden Spritz in the middle and Brennan's Champagne Cocktail at the top.

For a server it is a sales map. Offer the Champagne Cocktail to anyone celebrating, the Riviera to a guest who wants something light in the sun, the OBX to the gin drinker, the spritz to the aperitivo lover and the Bodrum to someone who does not care for wine. Confirm the hours on shift, since they can change.

card.front: When and where does Bubbles at Brennan's run?
card.back: In the Roost Bar and the courtyard, Monday to Friday, 2 to 6, with Champagne sabred on Fridays at 5. Five bubbly cocktails, rosé bottles and bar snacks.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)

components.name: The Roost's luxury cocktails
components.explain:
Three cocktails are poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, the house's bar: the Flamingo, the Birdcage and the Spoonbill. The house page calls them Luxury Roost Bar Cocktails and prints their bottles and prices; it prints no measures, glasses or garnishes, so those are confirmed with the bar.

All three names belong to birds or their keeping, which suits a bar called the Roost; the house has not published the reason, so a server tells no story about it.

The service rule matters more than the names. Because they are poured only in the Roost, a dining room server never brings one to the table. Mention them as an invitation: the Flamingo for a celebration, the Birdcage as a slow nightcap, the Spoonbill with its spoon of caviar for the start of a big evening.

card.front: Which three cocktails are poured only in the Roost?
card.back: The Flamingo, the Birdcage and the Spoonbill. From the dining room they are an invitation to the bar, never a drink brought to the table.

sources: pack notes on the Roost cocktails

components.name: The beach names at Bubbles
components.explain:
Three of the bubbly cocktails carry the names of seaside places, which suits a menu poured in a courtyard in the afternoon.

The Riviera calls up the sunny Mediterranean coast. Bodrum is a resort and yachting town on Turkey's Aegean coast, once the ancient Halicarnassus. OBX is the common shorthand for the Outer Banks, the barrier islands off North Carolina.

The menu says nothing about why these names were chosen, so a server tells no tale beyond what the names are. Used lightly, they are a pleasant way in: the Riviera for a guest who wants something light and French in feeling, the Bodrum for the rum lover, the OBX for the gin drinker who likes fruit with bubbles.

card.front: What places do the Riviera, Bodrum and OBX name?
card.back: The Mediterranean coast, a resort town on Turkey's Aegean coast, and the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The menu gives no reason for the names, so tell no story.

components.name: The spritz
components.explain:
The spritz comes from the Veneto in the nineteenth century, under Austrian rule, when soldiers and officials found the local wine too strong and asked for a splash of water in it; spritzen is German for to splash. In time the splash became soda, the wine became sparkling, and a bitter liqueur joined, and in the 1950s Aperol made the bright orange version famous.

A spritz is an aperitivo: low in strength, bittersweet and fizzy, drunk before a meal to wake the appetite.

The Chandon Garden Spritz follows that pattern with dry Chandon Brut and a bitter orange liqueur. Offer it to the guest who orders an aperitivo or an Aperol spritz, and call the wine sparkling wine, as the menu does, never Champagne.

card.front: Where does the word spritz come from?
card.back: From German spritzen, to splash: Austrian soldiers in the Veneto asked for water in strong wine. Now sparkling wine, a bitter liqueur and bubbles, drunk as an aperitivo.

components.name: New Orleans, a coffee city
components.explain:
New Orleans has been a coffee port since the early nineteenth century; by 1840 it was the second largest coffee importer in the United States, and coffee still arrives on its wharves.

The city's taste came with French habits. France had stretched coffee with roasted chicory root during Napoleon's Continental Blockade, and when the Union blockade cut imports during the Civil War, New Orleanians are said to have done the same; some historians call that last part possibly fabled. Either way the blend stayed, for its body and its gentle, cocoa-like bitterness.

So coffee at Brennan's is a local story, not an afterthought: chicory coffee closes the Traditional Breakfast beside the Bananas Foster, and the house's beans come from Congregation, a roaster across the river in Algiers Point.

card.front: Why does New Orleans drink coffee with chicory?
card.back: French habit and a great coffee port: chicory stretched coffee in Napoleon's blockade and, it is said, in the Civil War. It stayed for its body and cocoa-like bitterness.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)

components.name: Billboard Songs from 1946 and Temperance, 1946
components.explain:
The fall cocktail list is called Billboard Songs from 1946, and the menu says it celebrates 80 years at Brennan's, which opened in 1946. Every drink carries the title of a hit song of that year, and the two spirit-free drinks sit beside them under Temperance, 1946.

The list is built in pairs a server can sell. Rumors are Flying and Personality share tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup, one on rye and one on zero proof rosé. Old Buttermilk Sky and Oh! What It Seemed to Be are the same fig and egg white sour, one with tequila and one with Lyre's.

Song facts are a gentle table story; tell one only if the guest is curious. The menu's own spelling of each title is the one to say.

card.front: What do the fall drink names celebrate?
card.back: Hit songs of 1946, the year Brennan's opened: the list celebrates 80 years. Two spirit-free drinks sit beside it under Temperance, 1946.

items: Oh! What It Seemed to Be

components.name: The song For Sentimental Reasons
components.explain:
The full title is (I Love You) For Sentimental Reasons. The King Cole Trio's recording entered the Billboard Best Seller chart on 22 November 1946 and reached number one on 28 December 1946, Nat King Cole's first number one pop single.

It is a soft, romantic ballad, the sort of song a couple might have danced to in the year Brennan's opened.

The drink named for it is the gentlest on the fall list: sparkling wine over pear purée and allspice dram, fizzy and fruity with a warm spice at the end. That makes a natural line for a server: a sentimental, celebratory glass, the one to offer a couple marking an anniversary or a guest who usually orders bubbles.

card.front: Who took For Sentimental Reasons to number one, and when?
card.back: Nat King Cole with the King Cole Trio, number one on 28 December 1946, his first number one pop single. Ours is the gentle sparkling pear drink.

components.name: The song Prisoner of Love
components.explain:
Prisoner of Love is older than its hit year. Russ Columbo and Clarence Gaskill wrote the music in 1931, with words by Leo Robin. Perry Como recorded it in December 1945, and his version reached the Billboard charts on 30 March 1946, spent three weeks at number one from 4 May and finished as the top seller of the year on Billboard's year-end list.

The drink of the same name is the fall list's gin drink, made silky with clarified heavy cream and scented with Earl Grey tea and orange flower water.

The pairing is easy to tell: a smooth crooner's ballad and a smooth, fragrant drink. Keep the story short, and let the clarified cream be the real talking point.

card.front: Whose recording made Prisoner of Love a 1946 hit?
card.back: Perry Como's: number one for three weeks from May 1946 and the year's top seller. The song itself dates from 1931. Ours is the silky gin drink.

components.name: The song Rumors Are Flying
components.explain:
Rumors Are Flying was written by Bennie Benjamin and George David Weiss. Frankie Carle and His Orchestra took it to number one on the Billboard charts in October 1946, and it finished fifth on Billboard's list of the year's biggest sellers. The menu prints the title as Rumors are Flying, and that is how the drink is said.

It is a bright, bouncy dance band song, quick and full of gossip.

The drink is the fall list's whiskey drink, built on Brennan's barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye with tart cherry juice, brown sugar syrup and orange bitters, rich and spirit-forward. Offer it to the Old Fashioned drinker, and mention its spirit-free twin, Personality, for anyone at the table not drinking.

card.front: Which band had the 1946 hit with Rumors Are Flying?
card.back: Frankie Carle and His Orchestra, number one in October 1946. The menu prints Rumors are Flying for our barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye drink.

components.name: The song To Each His Own
components.explain:
To Each His Own was written by Jay Livingston and Ray Evans as the title song of a 1946 Paramount film, which won Olivia de Havilland an Academy Award. Eddy Howard and His Orchestra took it to number one on 3 August 1946 for eight weeks, and the Ink Spots and others had versions on the chart at the same moment, so several recordings shared the Top Ten.

The title fits a drink of personal taste. Ours is the fall list's orchard drink: Daron Fine Calvados, the apple brandy of Normandy, with Lillet Blanc and quince liqueur.

Offer it to the brandy or Cognac drinker who wants the season in a glass; the song is a pleasant aside if the guest asks about the name.

card.front: Which 1946 film gave us the song To Each His Own?
card.back: The Paramount film To Each His Own; Eddy Howard took the song to number one in August 1946. Ours is the Calvados, Lillet and quince drink.

components.name: The song Ole Buttermilk Sky
components.explain:
Hoagy Carmichael wrote Ole Buttermilk Sky with Jack Brooks and introduced it himself in the 1946 Western film Canyon Passage. Kay Kyser's recording made it a hit, reaching number one on 14 December 1946, and the song was nominated for an Academy Award.

The song is spelled Ole; the menu prints the drink as Old Buttermilk Sky, and a server says the menu's name for the drink. A buttermilk sky is a sky of small, rippled clouds.

The drink is the fall list's tequila sour, made with Volcán reposado, fig liqueur, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white, so it has a pale, silky foam on top, a nice echo of those soft clouds. Its spirit-free twin is Oh! What It Seemed to Be.

card.front: Who wrote the song behind Old Buttermilk Sky?
card.back: Hoagy Carmichael, with Jack Brooks, for the 1946 film Canyon Passage; Kay Kyser had the number one. The song is spelled Ole; our menu prints Old.

components.name: The song Five Minutes More
components.explain:
Five Minutes More was written in 1946 by Sammy Cahn, words, and Jule Styne, music. Frank Sinatra's recording reached number one on 14 September 1946 and stayed there for four weeks, ending the year fourth on Billboard's list.

The song is a plea to stay a little longer, which makes an easy line at the end of an evening.

The drink is the fall list's herbal one: Cathead mandarin vodka with Green Chartreuse, Licor 43 and lemon, bright, layered and strong, best sipped slowly. Offer it to a guest who loves herbal liqueurs, or to the vodka drinker who wants more character, perhaps as the reason to stay five minutes more.

card.front: Who sang the 1946 number one Five Minutes More?
card.back: Frank Sinatra, number one from 14 September 1946. Ours is the Cathead mandarin vodka drink with Green Chartreuse, Licor 43 and lemon.

components.name: The song Personality
components.explain:
Personality was written by Johnny Burke and Jimmy Van Heusen for the 1946 film Road to Utopia, where Dorothy Lamour sang it. Johnny Mercer and the Pied Pipers made it a number one record for the week of 9 March 1946.

It is a playful, witty song, and the drink named for it sits under Temperance, 1946, the spirit-free side of the list.

The drink is a zero proof Wölffer Estate sparkling rosé with tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup, bright and fizzy. It shares its cherry and brown sugar with Rumors are Flying, so a couple can order the same idea with and without spirit. It lets a guest who is not drinking join any toast.

card.front: Which film first featured the song Personality?
card.back: Road to Utopia, 1946, sung by Dorothy Lamour; Johnny Mercer's record was number one in March 1946. Ours is the spirit-free sparkling rosé drink.

components.name: The song Oh! What It Seemed to Be
components.explain:
Oh! What It Seemed to Be was written by Bennie Benjamin, George Weiss and Frankie Carle. In 1946 it reached number one twice over, for Frankie Carle's orchestra and for Frank Sinatra, and between them the two recordings held the top of the charts for a large part of the year.

The title is wistful, a look back at how things seemed, and the drink sits under Temperance, 1946, the spirit-free list.

It is the twin of Old Buttermilk Sky: Lyre's non-alcoholic agave spirit with fig syrup, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white, a silky sour without spirit. Because Lyre's is labelled under 0.5 percent alcohol, a server says non-alcoholic, never alcohol free.

card.front: Who took Oh! What It Seemed to Be to number one?
card.back: Both Frankie Carle's orchestra and Frank Sinatra, in 1946. Ours is the spirit-free sour, twin of Old Buttermilk Sky; say non-alcoholic, not alcohol free.

items: Oh! What It Seemed to Be

components.name: Zero proof and non-alcoholic
components.explain:
Spirit-free drinks need exact words, because guests who avoid alcohol rely on them. Zero proof is a marketing term, not a legal one and not a guarantee of 0.0; some zero proof products carry a trace. Non-alcoholic, in American labelling, allows under 0.5 percent.

The two drinks under Temperance, 1946 show the difference. Personality is built on Wölffer Estate's zero proof sparkling rosé; confirm the figure on its label at lineup. Oh! What It Seemed to Be is built on Lyre's agave, which Lyre's labels under 0.5 percent, so a server says non-alcoholic, never alcohol free or zero.

Each has a spirited twin on the fall list, Rumors are Flying and Old Buttermilk Sky, so a whole table can share an idea. Any question about pregnancy, medication or recovery is answered with the label and the bar, never a promise from the server.

card.front: Which spirit-free drink do we call non-alcoholic rather than zero?
card.back: Oh! What It Seemed to Be: Lyre's is labelled under 0.5 percent. Personality uses a zero proof rosé; confirm its label figure at lineup.

components.name: The dessert cocktails
components.explain:
The dessert menu prints three dessert cocktails: Floating in South Africa, a root beer float with Amarula; the Apple Crumble, bourbon with apple cider, butterscotch, maple and cinnamon; and Banane au Chocolat, banana and chocolate liqueurs with Pedro Ximénez sherry. Beside them sit the coffee cocktails.

A dessert cocktail is a drink that can stand in for a plate, sweet and rich enough to close a meal on its own, or to share beside a dessert.

For a server they solve a common moment: the table that is too full for another plate but not ready to leave. Offer the float to a birthday table, the Apple Crumble to the bourbon drinker in the fall, and Banane au Chocolat to the chocolate lover or anyone who loved the Bananas Foster.

card.front: What are the three dessert cocktails, and when do we offer them?
card.back: Floating in South Africa, the Apple Crumble and Banane au Chocolat. Offer them when a table is too full for another plate but not ready to leave.

components.name: Shaking
components.explain:
Shaking means sealing the drink in a tin with plenty of ice and shaking it hard for several seconds. It chills, dilutes and aerates at once, so a drink with cream, juice or liqueur comes out cold, lightened and smooth, with a fine froth.

The rule bartenders learn first: shake what is cloudy, stir what is clear. Cream, citrus, egg and purée need the violence of the shake to marry; a drink of spirits alone is stirred so it stays silky.

At Brennan's the guide prints the Brandy Milk Punch as shaken with heavy cream and vanilla bean. For the sours, the creamy drinks and the espresso martini the menu prints no method, so shaking is the classic way and the bar confirms its own build before a server describes it.

card.front: Shake or stir: what is the bartender's rule?
card.back: Shake what is cloudy, stir what is clear. Cream, citrus, egg and purée are shaken to chill, dilute and froth; spirit-only drinks are stirred to stay silky.

components.name: Stirring
components.explain:
Stirring is done in a mixing glass with ice and a long bar spoon, turned smoothly for twenty or thirty seconds until the drink is cold and has taken on just enough water. It adds no air, so a drink of spirit, sugar and bitters stays clear, dense and silky.

That is why the Sazerac is stirred, never shaken: it is all spirit, and it is strained into its glass with no ice, so the dilution in the stir is all the water it will ever get.

At Brennan's the guide prints the Classic Sazerac as stirred with Peychaud's. Thompson's Dream and the Origin Story follow the same pattern, and an Old Fashioned style drink like the Birdcage is a stirred family too. Confirm each build with the bar.

card.front: Why is a Sazerac stirred and never shaken?
card.back: It is all spirit: stirring chills and dilutes without adding air, so it stays clear and silky. It is strained into a glass with no ice.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: The rinse
components.explain:
A rinse is a small measure of a strongly flavoured spirit swirled round a chilled glass to coat it, with the excess poured away, before the drink goes in. The guest gets the spirit's perfume on every sip without much of its taste.

In the classic Sazerac build two glasses are used: one is packed with ice to chill while the drink is stirred in the other. The serving glass is emptied, coated with the anise spirit and drained, and the stirred drink is strained into it, with no ice.

At Brennan's the Classic is rinsed with Herbsaint and Thompson's Dream with St. George absinthe; the Origin Story carries Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe in the same pattern. The bar confirms its own steps.

card.front: What does a rinse give a drink?
card.back: The aroma of a strong spirit without much of its flavour: the chilled glass is coated, the excess poured away, then the drink strained in with no ice.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Rolling a Bloody Mary
components.explain:
Rolling means pouring a drink back and forth between two tins, or a tin and a glass, several times with ice. It chills and mixes without the violence of a shake.

Bartenders roll a Bloody Mary because shaking tomato whips air into it, turning it thin and foamy and breaking its texture. Rolled, it stays thick and smooth, with the spice evenly through it.

The menu prints no method for either of the house's tomato drinks, so rolling is the classic technique a server can explain, not a promise of the house build. The Bloody Bull adds beef bouillon to the house mix, and the Bloody Mary comes with pickled okra and spicy beans; the bar confirms how each is built and served.

card.front: Why do bartenders roll a Bloody Mary rather than shake it?
card.back: Shaking whips air into tomato and leaves it thin and foamy. Rolling between two tins chills and mixes it while keeping it thick and smooth.

components.name: The dry shake
components.explain:
A dry shake is a shake without ice, used for drinks with egg white. Shaken warm, the egg white's proteins unfold and trap air, whipping into a foam rather like a soft meringue. The bartender then adds ice and shakes again to chill and dilute. In the reverse dry shake the order is swapped, ice first, then a shake without it.

The result is the pale, velvety cap on a sour and the silky body under it; the egg white adds texture, not flavour.

Two Brennan's drinks print egg white: Old Buttermilk Sky and its spirit-free twin, Oh! What It Seemed to Be. The menu prints no method, so the dry shake is the classic technique and the bar confirms its build. Any question about egg goes to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What is a dry shake, and why is it done?
card.back: Shaking egg white without ice so it whips into a fine foam, then shaking again with ice to chill. It gives a sour its silky body and pale cap.

components.name: Floating the cream
components.explain:
Floating is laying a lighter liquid on top of a heavier one so the two stay apart. For an Irish coffee, cream is whipped only until it thickens to a pourable ribbon, then poured slowly over the back of a spoon onto the hot, sweetened coffee.

Sugar does real work here: dissolved in the coffee it makes the coffee denser, which helps the cream sit on top. Once the cream is on, the drink is never stirred; the guest sips the hot coffee through the cool cream.

At Brennan's the guide prints the Irish Coffee built in the glass, sugar into the chicory coffee, then the whiskey, then the cream floated and left alone. The coffee with Frangelico and Nocello also carries whipped cream; whether it is floated or piped is a question for the bar.

card.front: Why is an Irish coffee never stirred once the cream is on?
card.back: The cream is floated to stay on top: the guest sips hot coffee through cool cream. Sugar dissolved in the coffee makes it denser and helps the float.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Building in the glass
components.explain:
To build a drink is to make it in the glass it is served in, ingredient by ingredient, with no shaker or mixing glass. It suits drinks that would lose their bubbles or their layers if mixed hard.

Order matters. An Irish coffee is built hot: sugar dissolved in the coffee, then whiskey, then the cream. A Champagne Cocktail starts with the bitters-soaked sugar cube in the glass and the wine poured gently over it so it keeps its sparkle. Highballs and spritzes are built the same way, the sparkling part going in last.

At Brennan's the guide prints the Irish Coffee as built in the glass, and the Champagne Cocktail's printed build is the classic one. The bar confirms the rest.

card.front: What does it mean to build a drink?
card.back: To make it in its serving glass, ingredient by ingredient, no shaker. Order matters: sugar, then spirit, then cream for an Irish coffee; cube first, Champagne poured over.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Topping with bubbles
components.explain:
Many drinks are finished with something sparkling: Champagne, another sparkling wine or sparkling water. The rule is to add it last and gently, down the side of the glass, never shaking it, so it keeps its fizz.

The bubbles lift aroma out of the glass and lighten a drink, making a liqueur or a purée feel fresh rather than heavy. Brut, meaning dry, wines keep a drink crisp; a softly sweet one like the Bigaro rounds it.

At Brennan's this runs through Bubbles and the fall list: Taittinger in the Flamingo, Champagne in the Champagne Cocktail, sparkling wine in the Riviera and For Sentimental Reasons, Chandon Brut in the spritz, the Bigaro in the OBX, sparkling water in the Bodrum and a zero proof rosé in Personality.

card.front: How is a sparkling top added to a cocktail?
card.back: Last and gently, down the side of the glass, never shaken, so it keeps its fizz. The bubbles lift aroma and lighten the drink.

components.name: Smoking a cocktail
components.explain:
A smoked cocktail is a drink given the aroma of wood smoke just before it is served. Bars do it in several ways: by trapping smoke from burning wood chips in the glass or under a cloche, by smoking the glass before the drink goes in, or with a handheld smoking gun.

The smoke sits mostly in the aroma, so the first thing the guest meets is the scent of the fire, then the drink underneath. Darker spirits such as bourbon carry it best, because their oak and caramel already lean that way.

The Birdcage is the Roost's smoked Old Fashioned. The house page prints the bourbon, bitters, orange and cherry but not how the bar smokes it, so a server describes the smoke and lets the bar explain the method.

card.front: How is the Birdcage made smoky?
card.back: It is smoked just before service, so smoke meets the guest first. The house page does not say how; ask the bar, and describe aroma, not method.

components.name: Clarifying with cream
components.explain:
Clarifying a drink with milk or cream is the old milk punch technique. The spirit and acidic ingredients, such as citrus or tea, are added to the milk or cream, which curdles. Left to rest and then strained slowly through cloth, the curds catch the cloudy parts and the liquid runs clear.

What comes through is translucent and silky, without the weight of cream, and keeps far better than a creamy drink; the curds also soften any harsh edges.

The Prisoner of Love prints clarified heavy cream with gin, Earl Grey tea and orange flower water. How the bar clarifies it and for how long are questions for the bar, and any question about cream goes to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What does clarifying with cream do to a drink?
card.back: Acid curdles the cream, the curds are strained out through cloth, and the drink runs clear and silky. It is the old milk punch technique, used in the Prisoner of Love.

components.name: Barrel ageing
components.explain:
Barrel ageing means resting a spirit, a finished cocktail or even bitters in an oak cask. The wood softens sharp edges and adds vanilla, caramel and spice, and a little evaporation concentrates what is left. A used spirit cask lends some of its old contents too.

Two Brennan's drinks print it. Rumors are Flying is built on Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye, and the Origin Story uses barrel-aged Peychaud's.

What the menu does not print is who did the ageing, in what cask and for how long. Those are questions for the bar, so a server says barrel-aged for Brennan's and no more until the bar gives the story. Guests often ask; it is worth asking at lineup.

card.front: What does barrel ageing add, and what do we not know?
card.back: Oak softens and adds vanilla, caramel and spice. Who aged our Rittenhouse and Peychaud's, in what cask and how long, is a question for the bar.

components.name: The sour pattern
components.explain:
A sour is the oldest pattern behind most shaken cocktails: a spirit, a sour part, usually lemon or lime, and a sweet part, often with egg white for body. The bartender balances sharp against sweet so neither wins.

Learn the pattern and most of the fall list reads at a glance. Old Buttermilk Sky is a tequila sour, with fig liqueur and cinnamon syrup on the sweet side and lemon on the sour. Oh! What It Seemed to Be is the same sour without spirit. Five Minutes More is a vodka sour sweetened by two liqueurs, and the Apple Crumble balances butterscotch and maple with lemon.

Telling a guest it is a sour gives them a map: bright, balanced and refreshing rather than sweet or strong.

card.front: What are the three parts of a sour?
card.back: A spirit, a sour part such as lemon, and a sweet part, often with egg white. Old Buttermilk Sky and Five Minutes More follow the pattern.

components.name: Cold brew
components.explain:
Cold brew is coffee made without heat. Coarse ground coffee is steeped in cold or room temperature water for twelve to twenty-four hours, then strained. It is not hot coffee poured over ice; it is a different extraction.

Because heat never touches it, fewer of the sharp, acidic and bitter compounds come out, so cold brew tastes smoother, rounder and naturally a little sweeter than iced hot coffee.

The Café Glacé de la Maison starts with chicory cold brew, which makes it smooth and roasty, then a cardamom-clove syrup and an orange flower foam. It is the guide's zero-proof pick for the baked apple, the turtle soup and the duck confit waffle, and the drink to offer anyone skipping the milk punch.

card.front: How is cold brew made, and how does it taste?
card.back: Coarse coffee steeped in cold water for 12 to 24 hours, then strained. Smoother, rounder and less acidic than iced hot coffee; the base of our Café Glacé.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)

components.name: Cold pressing
components.explain:
Cold pressing is a way of making juice without heat or fast spinning blades. The fruit is ground to a pulp and pressed hard, often in a cloth, so the juice is squeezed out slowly and stays cool.

Juice made this way keeps more of the fresh fruit's colour and bright flavour; because it is not pasteurised by heat, it is usually kept cold and has a short life.

The Revive Cold-Pressed Juice is listed under juices that are locally made and fresh squeezed: strawberry, apple and pineapple. Who presses it for Brennan's is not printed, and a search could not confirm the maker, so that is a question for the bar. It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine.

card.front: What does cold pressed mean on our juice?
card.back: The fruit is pressed slowly without heat, keeping colour and fresh flavour. Ours is strawberry, apple and pineapple; who presses it is a question for the bar.

components.name: Coffee service at the table
components.explain:
Coffee closes most meals at Brennan's, so it is served with care. Ask how the guest takes it before it arrives, bring cream and sugar unasked if they take them, and pour or set the cup so the handle faces the guest's right hand.

Know the three coffees and what makes each different. The New Orleans-style coffee carries chicory, roasty with a gentle bitterness that balances dessert. The Congregation single origin has no chicory and tastes of one place; read today's origin from the coffee card on shift. The Café Glacé is cold brew, cold and lightly sweet.

The guide pairs chicory coffee with six sweet plates, so offering coffee as dessert menus go down is part of the sale, not an afterthought.

card.front: What do you ask before bringing a guest coffee?
card.back: How they take it, so cream and sugar arrive with it. Then know the choice: chicory coffee, the single origin without chicory, or the cold Café Glacé.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)

components.name: Brandy
components.explain:
Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine, or from other fermented fruit, and usually aged in oak. Cognac is France's best-known grape brandy, made under strict rules; Calvados is Normandy's apple brandy.

Aged brandy brings dried fruit, vanilla and a soft warmth, rounder than whiskey and less sharp than vodka, which is why it suits cream so well.

The Brandy Milk Punch prints simply brandy, so a server says brandy and does not name a house or a grade until the bar confirms one. Brandy is the spirit of the New Orleans milk punch tradition; the bourbon version is the other well-known style. The Origin Story is built on a named Cognac, Dudognon, and To Each His Own on Daron Fine Calvados.

card.front: What is brandy, and which brandy is in our milk punch?
card.back: A spirit distilled from wine or fruit, usually oak aged. The menu prints only brandy for the milk punch, so name no house or grade until the bar confirms it.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Heavy cream
components.explain:
Heavy cream is the richest pouring cream, high enough in butterfat to shake into a light froth or whip into peaks. In a cocktail it gives body, softens alcohol and carries flavours such as vanilla, nutmeg and pistachio.

Cream drinks are shaken hard with ice so the cream lightens and chills; they are best made fresh and served at once.

The guide prints the Brandy Milk Punch as shaken with heavy cream and vanilla bean, which makes it cold, creamy and smooth, like a lighter eggnog without the egg. The Bodrum prints cream too, with pistachio, lime and sparkling water. Both carry dairy as printed, so any question about cream goes to the service note and lineup, never a guess.

card.front: What does heavy cream do in our milk punch?
card.back: Gives body, softens the brandy and carries the vanilla and nutmeg; shaken hard, it turns cold, frothy and smooth. Dairy questions go to the service note.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Vanilla bean
components.explain:
Vanilla comes from the cured seed pod of a climbing orchid. Picked green, the pods are sweated and dried for months until they turn dark and fragrant, full of tiny black seeds.

A real bean gives a deeper, more floral and warmer perfume than extract. In a bar it is usually steeped ahead in the cream or a syrup, so the flavour is ready for every shake.

The menu prints vanilla bean, not extract, for the Brandy Milk Punch, and a server can say so with pride; how the bar uses the bean is a question for lineup. Vanilla is also the backbone of the housemade vanilla bean ice cream in Floating in South Africa, and Licor 43 in Five Minutes More leans on it.

card.front: Vanilla bean or extract: what does our milk punch use?
card.back: Real vanilla bean, as the menu prints: warmer and more floral than extract. How the bar steeps it is a question for lineup.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Nutmeg
components.explain:
Nutmeg is the seed of a tropical evergreen tree; mace is the lacy red covering around it. Grated fresh, it gives a warm, sweet, slightly woody perfume that fades fast once ground, which is why bartenders grate it over the drink at the last moment.

It is the classic finish for cream drinks: milk punch, eggnog and the Brandy Alexander all wear it.

On the Brandy Milk Punch the menu prints nutmeg and the guide says it tops the drink. The dusting is the first thing the guest smells as the glass comes up, and the first thing a guest sees. Describe it as fresh nutmeg on top only once the bar has confirmed it grates fresh.

card.front: What tops the Brandy Milk Punch, and why grate it fresh?
card.back: Nutmeg. Freshly grated it gives a warm, sweet perfume that fades quickly once ground, so it goes on at the last moment.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Vodka
components.explain:
Vodka is a neutral spirit distilled to high strength from grain, potatoes or other starches, then filtered and cut with water. It is meant to be clean, with little taste of its own beyond a soft texture and a hint of the grain or potato.

That cleanness is its job in a cocktail: it carries other flavours without fighting them, which is why it anchors the Bloody Mary and the espresso martini.

At Brennan's the menus name a brand only in some drinks. The Bloody Bull, the Bloody Mary and the Espresso Martini print vodka alone, so which vodka is a question for the bar. The Flamingo names Chopin, a Polish potato vodka, and Five Minutes More names Cathead's mandarin vodka from Mississippi.

card.front: Which of our drinks name their vodka?
card.back: The Flamingo names Chopin and Five Minutes More names Cathead mandarin. The Bloody Bull, Bloody Mary and Espresso Martini print vodka only; ask the bar which.

components.name: Housemade Bloody Mary mix
components.explain:
A Bloody Mary mix is the seasoned tomato base of the drink. Classic mixes are tomato juice with lemon, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, horseradish, celery salt and black pepper, made ahead so every drink tastes the same.

Ours is printed as housemade on both tomato drinks. The guide sets the heat by the mix and notes that Bloody Mary mixes usually include Worcestershire, which is made with anchovy; that is a general warning, not a confirmed fact about this mix.

So the server's job is to say housemade and stop there. What goes in it, how hot it runs today and whether the Bloody Bull and the Bloody Mary share one batch are questions for the bar, and any question about fish or spice goes to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What do we tell a guest about our Bloody Mary mix?
card.back: That it is housemade. Its recipe, today's heat and whether both tomato drinks share it are bar questions; Worcestershire questions go to the service note and lineup.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Beef bouillon
components.explain:
Bouillon is French for broth: a clear, savoury stock made by simmering beef, bones and vegetables, strained clean. Cold beef bouillon has a rich, meaty depth with no fat on it.

In a drink it turns a Bloody Mary into something closer to a spicy, chilled consommé, which is how the guide describes the Bloody Bull. The idea comes from the Bull Shot of 1952, vodka and canned beef bouillon.

At Brennan's it is the reason the Bloody Bull pours with the turtle soup on the Traditional Breakfast. It also means the drink carries beef: the guide's service note says so plainly and offers the Brennan's Bloody Mary instead. Whether the bouillon is a house stock is a question for the bar.

card.front: What does beef bouillon add to the Bloody Bull?
card.back: A clear, savoury beef broth: it makes the drink rich and meaty, like a spicy chilled consommé. It carries beef; the Bloody Mary is the alternative.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Pickled okra and spicy beans
components.explain:
Okra is a green seed pod that came to the American South from Africa through the slave trade, now a staple of Louisiana cooking from gumbo to the pickle jar. Pickled whole in vinegar with spice, it stays crisp and loses the slipperiness okra has when cooked.

Spicy beans in the Gulf South usually means pickled green beans with chilli; the menu prints only spicy beans, so say it as printed.

On Brennan's Bloody Mary the menu prints both as the garnish, standing in the glass. They give the drink its pickled crunch and a local accent, and they are the easy way to tell it apart from the Bloody Bull. Which vegetables and how hot are confirmed with the bar.

card.front: What garnishes Brennan's Bloody Mary?
card.back: Pickled okra and spicy beans, as the menu prints: a crisp, tangy, local garnish that sets it apart from the Bloody Bull.

components.name: Rye whiskey
components.explain:
American rye whiskey is distilled from a mash of at least 51 percent rye and aged in new charred oak. Rye gives a drier, spicier, more peppery whiskey than bourbon's sweet corn, with notes of baking spice and dark bread.

That spice is why rye became the Sazerac's spirit once cognac grew scarce, and why it suits stirred, spirit-forward drinks.

Brennan's pours three named ryes. The Classic Sazerac uses Sazerac rye, a Sazerac Company brand. Thompson's Dream uses Willett 4-year rye from Bardstown, bigger and hotter. Rumors are Flying uses Brennan's barrel-aged Rittenhouse, a bottled in bond rye. Each step up the ladder brings more spice and heat.

card.front: How does rye differ from bourbon?
card.back: Rye is at least 51 percent rye grain: drier, spicier and more peppery than corn-sweet bourbon. It became the Sazerac's spirit once cognac grew scarce.

components.name: Sazerac rye whiskey
components.explain:
Sazerac Rye is the straight rye whiskey made under the Sazerac name by the Sazerac Company, the New Orleans firm that grew from Thomas Handy's Sazerac Coffee House business. It is a softer, rounder style of rye, spicy with a little caramel.

The same company owns Peychaud's bitters and Herbsaint, so the Classic Sazerac at Brennan's is three bottles from one New Orleans family of brands in one glass: Sazerac rye, Peychaud's and a Herbsaint rinse.

That makes a good table line, and it explains the price: the Classic is the first rung at its price, before Thompson's Dream and the Origin Story. Measures and the sugar are confirmed with the bar.

card.front: What links Sazerac rye, Peychaud's and Herbsaint?
card.back: All three are Sazerac Company brands, so the Classic Sazerac is one New Orleans family of bottles in a single glass.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Peychaud's bitters
components.explain:
Peychaud's is a bright red New Orleans aromatic bitters, made first by Antoine Peychaud in his Royal Street apothecary in the 1850s and now by the Sazerac Company. Bitters are spirit infused with bitter roots, barks and spices; a few dashes season a drink the way salt seasons food.

Peychaud's is lighter and more floral than Angostura, with anise and cherry, and it gives the Sazerac its rosy colour. A Sazerac with Angostura instead is a different drink.

At Brennan's the Classic is stirred with Peychaud's. The Origin Story uses barrel-aged Peychaud's, softened in oak; who ages it is a question for the bar. Thompson's Dream swaps in Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, a German tribute to the same style.

card.front: How do Peychaud's bitters differ from Angostura?
card.back: Peychaud's is red, lighter and more floral, with anise and cherry, and it colours the Sazerac. Angostura is darker and spicier, in the Old Fashioned and Champagne Cocktail.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Herbsaint
components.explain:
Herbsaint is New Orleans' own anise liqueur. J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learned absinthe making in France during the First World War, created it in New Orleans in 1934, after Prohibition and while absinthe was banned. It was sold first as Legendre Absinthe, though it held no grand wormwood; the federal authorities objected, and it became Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood.

The Sazerac Company bought the firm in 1949. The H is silent: ERB-sant.

In the Classic Sazerac it is only a rinse, so the guest gets its anise perfume without much of its flavour. The guide calls it our local anise liqueur: local by birth and ownership, though it is not distilled in the city today.

card.front: What is Herbsaint, and when was it created?
card.back: New Orleans' anise liqueur, created in 1934 as an absinthe substitute while absinthe was banned. Say ERB-sant; it rinses the Classic Sazerac glass.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: St. George Absinthe Verte
components.explain:
St. George Absinthe Verte comes from St. George Spirits in Alameda, California. Released after the federal rules changed in 2007, it was the first legal American absinthe since the 1912 ban.

It is built on brandy and flavoured with wormwood, star anise and fennel, then coloured and perfumed with herbs such as lemon balm, hyssop, meadowsweet, basil, mint, tarragon and stinging nettle. At 60 percent alcohol it is herbal and green rather than candied.

In Thompson's Dream it rinses the glass in place of the Classic's Herbsaint, so the drink smells greener and more herbal. Alongside the bigger Willett rye and the Creole bitters, that is the honest description of what the extra money buys.

card.front: What makes St. George absinthe special?
card.back: It was the first legal American absinthe after the ban ended in 2007: a brandy base, wormwood and garden herbs. It rinses Thompson's Dream.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe
components.explain:
Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is an absinthe supérieure made at the Combier distillery in Saumur, in France's Loire Valley. Wormwood and other plants are macerated in wine alcohol and distilled in old alembics; it is bottled at 68 percent.

It was made as a tribute by a native New Orleanian to the city's nineteenth-century absinthe culture, when the French Quarter's absinthe houses were famous, long before the ban. On the nose it is gentle fennel and fresh herbs with a long, soft anise finish.

In the Origin Story it brings a floral wormwood aroma to the cognac drink, in place of the Classic's Herbsaint. Whether the bar rinses with it, as the Sazerac pattern suggests, is confirmed at lineup.

card.front: What is Jade Nouvelle-Orléans, and which drink uses it?
card.back: A French absinthe from the Combier distillery in Saumur, made as a tribute to New Orleans' old absinthe culture. It perfumes the Origin Story.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Bitter Truth Creole Bitters
components.explain:
The Bitter Truth is a bitters maker from Munich. Its Creole Bitters are bright red, made in the New Orleans style with anise, caraway and fennel, plus cinnamon, pepper and dried fruit notes; they are sold as a natural choice for a Sazerac and an alternative to Peychaud's.

They are called Creole, not Peychaud's, because Peychaud's is a brand of its own.

In Thompson's Dream they take the Classic's Peychaud's role. With the louder Willett rye and the St. George absinthe rinse, the result is spicier and more herbal, though still recognisably a Sazerac. A useful guest line: a German bitters maker's tribute to the New Orleans style, made for exactly this drink.

card.front: What bitters go in Thompson's Dream?
card.back: Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, from Munich: red, with anise, caraway and fennel, a tribute to the New Orleans style in place of Peychaud's.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Willett 4-year rye
components.explain:
Willett is a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, founded in 1936 on the family farm. After the old distillery closed in the 1980s, the family began distilling on the site again in 2012, and its 4-year rye comes from that new production.

The family estate bottlings are known for being strong and spicy, bottled well above the Classic's rye; read the exact proof on the bottle at the bar rather than quoting one from memory.

In Thompson's Dream that strength is the point: a Sazerac with louder rye spice and more heat, for the guest who already loves the Classic. It is the drink to offer whenever a guest orders a second Sazerac.

card.front: Why does Willett rye make Thompson's Dream louder?
card.back: It is a strong, spicy Bardstown rye from a family distillery founded in 1936, bottled higher than the Classic's rye; ask the bar for today's proof.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Dudognon Cognac
components.explain:
Cognac is grape brandy from the Cognac region of western France, double distilled in copper pot stills and aged in oak. Its best cru is Grande Champagne, chalky country that gives long, fine spirits; the name has nothing to do with the sparkling wine region.

The Dudognon family has grown grapes at Lignières-Sonneville, in the heart of Grande Champagne, since 1776. It is a traditional estate that distils only its own grapes and sells its spirits by age, such as a 10-year Réserve and a 20-year Vieille Réserve.

The Origin Story prints Dudognon Cognac without naming the bottling, so which one the bar pours is a lineup question. It gives the drink grape, dried fruit and oak, rounder than rye.

card.front: Where does Dudognon Cognac come from?
card.back: A family estate at Lignières-Sonneville in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first cru, growing grapes there since 1776. Which bottling we pour is a lineup question.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Chicory
components.explain:
Chicory is a hardy plant whose root is dried, roasted and ground. Brewed with coffee it adds body, a dark colour and a roasty, cocoa-like bitterness, and it carries no caffeine of its own.

The French used it to stretch coffee during Napoleon's blockade, and New Orleans, a French city and a great coffee port, kept the habit; the Civil War blockade is said to have fixed it.

Chicory runs through the Brennan's coffee list. The New Orleans-style coffee is blended with it, the Irish Coffee and the walnut and hazelnut coffee use the dark roast with chicory, the Café Glacé is chicory cold brew, and the Espresso Martini prints chicory. How it goes into the martini is a question for the bar.

card.front: What is chicory, and what does it add to coffee?
card.back: The roasted root of a hardy plant: body, dark colour and a roasty, cocoa-like bitterness, with no caffeine of its own. New Orleans blends it into its coffee.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)
guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Congregation Coffee
components.explain:
Congregation Coffee is a New Orleans roaster with its café at 240 Pelican Avenue in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter. It was founded in 2015; in 2023 it ceased operations while seeking new owners, and reopened in November 2023 under Brennan family ownership, roasting on Tchoupitoulas Street.

The breakfast tasting pours Brennan's private blend from Congregation with chicory, and the coffee list carries a Congregation single origin.

Single origin means the beans come from one place, so the cup tastes of that place rather than a blend, and there is no chicory. Congregation rotates its origins with the seasons, so read today's from the coffee card on shift, never from memory.

card.front: Where is Congregation Coffee, and what is single origin?
card.back: A roaster with its café in Algiers Point. Single origin means beans from one place, no blend and no chicory; read today's origin from the card.
