components.name: Brown sugar and brown sugar syrup
components.explain:
Brown sugar is sugar that keeps some of its molasses, which gives it a soft, caramel and toffee flavour and a darker colour than white sugar. Dissolved with water it becomes brown sugar syrup, the bar's easy way to sweeten a cold drink.

In hot coffee it melts straight in; in cold drinks a syrup is used, because grains do not dissolve in the cold.

Brennan's uses it three times. In the Irish Coffee it sweetens the chicory coffee and helps the cream float. In Rumors are Flying and its spirit-free twin, Personality, a brown sugar syrup rounds the tart cherry juice, which is why a couple can order the same idea with and without spirit.

card.front: Which of our drinks use brown sugar?
card.back: The Irish Coffee, stirred into the hot chicory coffee, and Rumors are Flying and Personality, as a syrup rounding the tart cherry juice.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Tullamore D.E.W.
components.explain:
Tullamore D.E.W. is an Irish whiskey established in 1829 at Tullamore in County Offaly. The letters are the initials of Daniel Edmund Williams, who rose to manage and then own the original distillery, and they also spell the word dew.

It is a blend of the three Irish whiskey styles, pot still, malt and grain, and triple distilled, which makes it smooth, light and gently spicy, well suited to hot coffee.

In Brennan's Irish Coffee it is the named whiskey, with chicory coffee, brown sugar and whipped cream. When a guest asks what the letters mean, the answer is a small, true story to tell while the coffee is poured.

card.front: What do the letters in Tullamore D.E.W. stand for?
card.back: Daniel Edmund Williams, the manager who came to own the distillery. It is a smooth triple-distilled Irish blend, established in 1829, in our Irish Coffee.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Whipped cream
components.explain:
Whipped cream is cream beaten until it traps air and thickens. For coffee drinks it is usually whipped only lightly, to a soft, pourable ribbon that floats on hot coffee; a stiff, piped cap is a different texture.

Cool cream on hot coffee is the pleasure of these drinks: the guest sips the hot, sweet coffee through the cold cap. Stirring it in loses that.

At Brennan's whipped cream tops the Irish Coffee and the coffee with Frangelico and Nocello. The guide's Irish Coffee lines say a cap of whipped cream; whether the bar floats it soft or tops it firm is a question to settle at lineup. Questions about cream go to the service note.

card.front: How should whipped cream sit on our coffee cocktails?
card.back: On top, never stirred in: the guest sips hot coffee through cool cream. Whether it is floated soft or set firm is confirmed at lineup.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p38 and p39, the bar pages)

components.name: Chopin vodka
components.explain:
Chopin is a Polish single-ingredient vodka. Its best-known bottling is made only from potatoes grown in the Polish region of Podlasie and distilled four times at Siedlce; the brand also makes rye and wheat versions from a single grain each.

Potato vodka is fuller and rounder in texture than most grain vodkas, with a soft, creamy feel and a faint earthiness.

In the Flamingo it pairs with Monkey 47 gin under dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger Champagne. The house page prints Chopin Vodka without saying which bottling, so potato is the likely and usual one but not stated; confirm with the bar before saying potato.

card.front: What kind of vodka is Chopin?
card.back: A Polish single-ingredient vodka, best known in its potato bottling from Podlasie, round and creamy. Confirm the bottling before saying potato.

components.name: Monkey 47 gin
components.explain:
Monkey 47 is a dry gin from Germany's Black Forest, the Schwarzwald. Its name gives away its numbers: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. Beside juniper and citrus it uses local plants such as lingonberries, spruce shoots and cranberries, and it rests in earthenware before bottling.

The result is a big, aromatic gin, fruity, green and floral, that stands up in a drink with Champagne.

In the Flamingo it joins Chopin vodka, dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger La Française. The vodka gives body and the gin gives the botanical lift a guest notices first. It is a fine name to drop for a gin lover deciding whether to visit the Roost.

card.front: What do the 47s in Monkey 47 mean?
card.back: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol: a Black Forest gin with lingonberries and spruce. It gives the Flamingo its botanical lift.

components.name: Dragonfruit
components.explain:
Dragonfruit, or pitaya, is the fruit of a climbing cactus, with a bright pink or yellow skin covered in green-tipped scales. Inside, the flesh is white or deep magenta, speckled with tiny edible black seeds.

Its flavour is gentle, somewhere between kiwi and pear, mildly sweet, and the red-fleshed kind gives a vivid pink colour, which makes it a favourite in bright, festive drinks.

In the Flamingo it brings fruit and almost certainly the drink's colour, though how the bar uses it, fresh, as a purée or a syrup, and the colour of the flesh are not printed. Describe it as a soft tropical fruit and let the bar confirm the rest.

card.front: What does dragonfruit taste like?
card.back: Gently sweet, between kiwi and pear, from a cactus fruit; red-fleshed kinds give vivid pink colour. How the Flamingo uses it is confirmed with the bar.

components.name: Champagne
components.explain:
Champagne is sparkling wine from the Champagne region of north-east France, made from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier by the traditional method, with its second fermentation in the bottle and long ageing on the lees. Only wine from that region may carry the name.

Bottle ageing gives it fine, persistent bubbles and flavours of citrus, apple, brioche and toast, which is why it lifts a cocktail rather than just fizzing.

Two Brennan's drinks print Champagne by name. Brennan's Champagne Cocktail prints Champagne without a house, and the Flamingo prints Taittinger La Française. Other drinks print sparkling wine, and a server keeps the distinction exactly as the menu does.

card.front: When may a sparkling wine be called Champagne?
card.back: Only when it comes from Champagne in north-east France, made by the traditional method. Our menus print Champagne for two drinks; the rest say sparkling wine.

components.name: Taittinger La Française
components.explain:
Taittinger is a Champagne house in Reims, founded in 1734 and family owned since 1932, one of the grandes marques. Its Brut La Française is the non-vintage house style, unusual for its high share of Chardonnay, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, aged close to four years on the lees in the chalk cellars under Reims.

That Chardonnay makes it fresh, light and elegant, with citrus and brioche.

In the Flamingo it tops Chopin vodka, Monkey 47 gin, dragonfruit and lemon. Brennan's also lists Taittinger La Française as a 3 litre double magnum on the Birthday Bubbles list, so the name links the Roost cocktail to the cellar.

card.front: What is distinctive about Taittinger La Française?
card.back: A high share of Chardonnay, about 40 percent, for a fresh, elegant non-vintage Champagne from a Reims house founded in 1734. It tops the Flamingo.

components.name: Bourbon
components.explain:
Bourbon is American whiskey made from a mash of at least 51 percent corn and aged in new charred oak barrels. The corn and the new oak give it sweetness, vanilla, caramel and a soft roundness, rounder than rye.

Most bourbon comes from Kentucky, though it may be made anywhere in the United States.

Two Brennan's drinks use it. The Birdcage is built on Rabbit Hole Dareringer, a wheated Louisville bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks. The Apple Crumble prints bourbon without a brand, so which one is a question for the bar. Its caramel and vanilla are the bridge to the butterscotch, maple and apple in that drink.

card.front: What makes a whiskey bourbon?
card.back: At least 51 percent corn, aged in new charred oak, in the United States: sweet, with vanilla and caramel. The Birdcage names Rabbit Hole; the Apple Crumble does not.

components.name: Rabbit Hole Dareringer
components.explain:
Rabbit Hole is a distillery in Louisville, Kentucky. Dareringer is its straight bourbon of corn, malted wheat and malted barley, aged in new charred oak and then finished in casks that held Pedro Ximénez sherry; it is bottled at 93 proof.

The sherry finish adds dried fruit, raisin and dark berry notes and a little extra richness to the bourbon's vanilla and oak.

In the Birdcage that richness carries the smoke, the Angostura, the orange and the cherry of an Old Fashioned. A useful line for the Old Fashioned drinker: a bourbon with a sweet sherry finish, wrapped in smoke, poured only in the Roost.

card.front: What finish gives Dareringer its dried fruit notes?
card.back: Casks that held Pedro Ximénez sherry, after ageing in new oak. That rich, raisiny bourbon is the base of the smoked Birdcage.

components.name: Angostura bitters
components.explain:
Angostura is the world's best-known aromatic bitters, named for the town where it began as a tonic in the nineteenth century. It is a concentrated spirit of gentian and spices, dark red-brown, used a few dashes at a time.

It tastes of clove, cinnamon and bitter root, and it seasons a drink, pulling sweet and strong together.

At Brennan's it is in the Birdcage, the smoked Old Fashioned, and in the Champagne Cocktail, soaked into a demerara sugar cube. It is not in the Classic Sazerac, which uses Peychaud's; mixing the two up at the table is a common slip.

card.front: Which of our drinks use Angostura, and which do not?
card.back: The Birdcage and the Champagne Cocktail use Angostura, a dark, spicy aromatic bitters. The Classic Sazerac uses the red Peychaud's instead; never mix them up.

components.name: Orange and cherry
components.explain:
Orange and cherry are the classic finishing touches of an Old Fashioned. An orange peel is twisted over the drink to spray its oils, then often dropped in; a cocktail cherry, usually a dark, sweet preserved one, sits in the glass.

The peel's oil is aroma first, bright and bitter-sweet; the cherry adds a little sweetness at the end.

The Birdcage prints orange and cherry with Rabbit Hole Dareringer and Angostura. Whether they are a garnish, a peel, a muddled fruit or a cherry liqueur is not printed, so a server says orange and cherry, as the house page does, and lets the bar describe the build and garnish.

card.front: What do orange and cherry add to an Old Fashioned?
card.back: Orange peel adds bright aroma from its oils; the cherry adds a sweet finish. How the Birdcage uses them is not printed, so ask the bar.

components.name: Gin
components.explain:
Gin is a spirit flavoured above all with juniper, the small blue-black cone of a conifer, together with other botanicals such as coriander, citrus peel and angelica. Dry gin is the classic modern style: piney, citrus-bright and unsweetened.

Every gin has its own recipe, which is why the brand matters more with gin than with vodka.

Four Brennan's drinks use gin. The Flamingo names Monkey 47, from the Black Forest, the Spoonbill names Hendrick's, with cucumber and rose, and the OBX names Gentilly Gin, made in New Orleans. The Prisoner of Love prints only gin, so which one is a question for the bar.

card.front: Which botanical must every gin taste of?
card.back: Juniper. Each gin adds its own botanicals: Monkey 47 in the Flamingo, Hendrick's in the Spoonbill, Gentilly in the OBX; the Prisoner of Love's gin is unnamed.

components.name: Hendrick's gin
components.explain:
Hendrick's is a Scottish gin launched in 1999 by William Grant and Sons at Girvan. It is made in two stills of different design whose spirits are blended, and essences of Bulgarian rose and cucumber are added after distillation.

That cucumber and rose made it stand apart when it launched, and they give it a cool, fresh, floral character, softer than a classic juniper-led gin.

In the Spoonbill it meets Cap Corse Mattei Blanc quinquina and chive oil, with a spoon of caviar alongside. The cucumber links naturally to the green chive, and the rose to the aperitif wine, which is a neat way to explain why the drink tastes so cool and savoury.

card.front: What two flavours set Hendrick's gin apart?
card.back: Cucumber and rose, added after distillation: a cool, floral Scottish gin from 1999. In the Spoonbill they meet chive oil and caviar.

components.name: Cap Corse Mattei Blanc quinquina
components.explain:
A quinquina is a wine aperitif flavoured with cinchona bark, the source of quinine, which gives it a gentle bitterness. In 1872 Louis-Napoléon Mattei named his aperitif after Cap Corse, the northern peninsula of Corsica, blending local Vermentino and Muscat wine with cinchona, spices and cédrat, a thick-peeled citron.

Cap Corse Mattei Blanc is light, citrusy and softly bitter, and the house is still family owned.

The house page prints it as Cap Corse Mattei Blanc Quinquina vermouth; strictly it is a quinquina, a cousin of vermouth. In the Spoonbill it plays the vermouth's part in a martini-style drink with Hendrick's gin and chive oil, with a spoon of caviar served alongside.

card.front: What is a quinquina?
card.back: A wine aperitif flavoured with cinchona bark, the source of quinine, gently bitter. Cap Corse Mattei, from Corsica since 1872, plays the vermouth's part in the Spoonbill.

components.name: Chive oil
components.explain:
Chive oil is a bright green oil made by blending fresh chives with a neutral oil, then straining it clear. Kitchens use it to finish soups and plates with colour and a fresh, gently oniony note.

In a cocktail a few drops float on the surface or bead in the drink, so the guest gets a savoury, green aroma before the first sip.

In the Spoonbill it is the savoury link between the cool cucumber of Hendrick's gin and the salty spoon of caviar served beside the drink. How the bar makes it and how it is added are not printed; describe the flavour and let the bar describe the method.

card.front: What does chive oil add to the Spoonbill?
card.back: A bright green, gently oniony aroma that links the cucumber of Hendrick's to the salt of the caviar. How it is made and added is confirmed with the bar.

components.name: Caviar
components.explain:
Caviar is the salted roe of sturgeon. The eggs are separated from the membrane, lightly salted and packed; their size, colour and flavour depend on the species, and most caviar served today is from farmed sturgeon.

Good caviar tastes clean and briny, buttery and nutty, and the eggs pop softly on the tongue. It is served cold, traditionally on a non-metal spoon of mother of pearl or horn.

The Spoonbill comes with a spoon of caviar alongside, which makes the drink a moment. Which caviar, how much and how it is presented are confirmed with the bar; any question about fish or roe goes to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What is caviar, and how does it come with the Spoonbill?
card.back: Salted sturgeon roe, briny and buttery, served cold. The Spoonbill comes with a spoon of it alongside; which caviar is confirmed with the bar.

components.name: Demerara sugar cube
components.explain:
Demerara is a light brown, large-grained cane sugar with a gentle toffee note, named for the Demerara region of South America, where it was first made. Pressed into a cube it dissolves slowly.

In a Champagne Cocktail the cube is soaked in bitters, set in the glass and topped with Champagne. As it dissolves it sweetens the wine a little at a time, and its rough surface keeps sending a stream of bubbles up the glass.

Brennan's Champagne Cocktail prints a demerara sugar cube with Angostura and Champagne, the classic build. It gives a faint caramel sweetness that grows as the guest drinks, which is worth telling: the last sip is the sweetest.

card.front: Why does the Champagne Cocktail keep bubbling?
card.back: The bitters-soaked demerara cube dissolves slowly, and its rough surface keeps sending bubbles up the glass. It also sweetens the wine gradually.

components.name: Lillet Blanc
components.explain:
Lillet is a French wine aperitif from Podensac, south of Bordeaux, founded in 1872 by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet. It is about 85 percent Bordeaux wine, Semillon for the Blanc, and 15 percent citrus liqueurs made from orange peels.

The old Kina Lillet carried more quinine; in 1986 Lillet Blanc replaced it, lighter, fruitier and less bitter. It tastes of orange, honey and blossom, served cold.

Two Brennan's drinks use it. In the Riviera it is topped with sparkling wine and lemon, light and floral; the menu spells it Lilet, but the bottle is Lillet. In To Each His Own it softens Daron Calvados and quince liqueur.

card.front: What is Lillet Blanc made from?
card.back: Bordeaux wine, mostly Semillon, with about 15 percent citrus liqueurs: a light French aperitif from Podensac. It is in the Riviera and To Each His Own.

components.name: Sparkling wine
components.explain:
Sparkling wine is any wine with bubbles of carbon dioxide trapped in it. The best is made by a second fermentation in the bottle, the traditional method of Champagne; tank-fermented sparkling wines such as Prosecco are fresher and simpler.

Only wine from Champagne may be called Champagne, so a menu that prints sparkling wine is promising bubbles, not a region.

At Brennan's the Riviera and For Sentimental Reasons print sparkling wine without a name, so which wine is a question for the bar. The spritz names Chandon Brut, the OBX names the Bigaro and Personality uses a zero proof rosé. Say sparkling wine exactly where the menu does.

card.front: Why do some menus say sparkling wine, not Champagne?
card.back: Only wine from Champagne may carry that name. The Riviera and For Sentimental Reasons print sparkling wine; which one is a question for the bar.

components.name: Rum
components.explain:
Rum is distilled from sugar cane, usually from molasses, sometimes from fresh cane juice. White rums are light and clean; aged rums take colour and vanilla, caramel and spice from the barrel.

It is the spirit of the Caribbean and of tiki drinks, and it pairs naturally with lime, cream and nuts.

The Bodrum prints rum without naming one, with pistachio, cream, lime and sparkling water, so which rum is a question for the bar. It is the one bubbly cocktail lengthened with sparkling water rather than wine, which makes it the drink for a rum lover, or for a guest who does not care for wine.

card.front: Which rum is in the Bodrum?
card.back: The menu prints only rum, so which one is a question for the bar. It is the one Bubbles cocktail lengthened with sparkling water, not wine.

components.name: Pistachio
components.explain:
The pistachio is the seed of a small tree native to Iran and Central Asia, now grown widely in California, Iran and Turkey. Roasted, it tastes sweet, buttery and gently resinous, with a green colour that marks pistachio desserts.

In drinks it usually arrives as a syrup, an orgeat-style nut milk or a liqueur, because whole nuts cannot be shaken smooth.

The Bodrum prints pistachio with rum, cream, lime and sparkling water. How the pistachio goes in is not printed, so the bar confirms it. The guide's service note says pistachio and cream, as printed, and any question about nuts goes to that note and lineup, never a guess.

card.front: What do we say if a guest asks about the pistachio?
card.back: That the Bodrum prints pistachio and cream, and how the pistachio goes in is confirmed with the bar. Nut questions go to the service note and lineup.

sources: pack service note for the Bodrum

components.name: Fresh lemon and lime
components.explain:
Fresh citrus juice is the sour side of most cocktails. Lemon is sharp and clean; lime is sharper, greener and a little bitter. Bartenders squeeze it fresh each day, because bottled juice tastes flat and cooked.

Citrus balances sweetness from liqueurs and syrups, brightens fruit and wakes up the spirit; a peel twisted over a drink adds aroma from its oils as well.

Lemon is printed in seven Brennan's drinks: the Flamingo, the Riviera, the OBX, Old Buttermilk Sky, Five Minutes More, Oh! What It Seemed to Be and the Apple Crumble. The Bodrum prints lime. Whether each is juice, peel or both is confirmed with the bar.

card.front: What job does fresh lemon do in a cocktail?
card.back: It is the sour side: it balances sweet liqueurs and syrups and brightens fruit. Seven of our drinks print lemon; the Bodrum prints lime.

items: Oh! What It Seemed to Be

components.name: Gentilly Gin
components.explain:
Gentilly Gin is made in New Orleans by Seven Three Distilling Co., which opened in 2017 in Tremé; the name Seven Three is a nod to the city's 73 neighbourhoods, and Gentilly is one of them.

Its seventeen botanicals were inspired by the traiteurs, the old folk healers of south Louisiana, and include elderflower and persimmon; it is bottled at 87 proof, and the distillery also makes a barrel-aged version.

In the OBX it meets peach, lemon and the softly sweet Elio Perrone Bigaro. A local gin in a courtyard drink is a good story for a visitor; which Gentilly bottling the bar pours is worth confirming.

card.front: Who makes Gentilly Gin?
card.back: Seven Three Distilling Co. of New Orleans, opened in 2017 in Tremé; its botanicals were inspired by the traiteurs. It is the gin in the OBX.

components.name: Peach
components.explain:
The peach is a stone fruit first grown in China and now loved across the American South. A ripe peach is juicy, floral and honeyed, with a soft acidity.

In drinks it comes as fresh fruit, a purée or a liqueur, and it is happiest with sparkling wine: the Bellini is white peach and Prosecco.

The OBX prints peach with Gentilly Gin, lemon and Elio Perrone Bigaro, whose Moscato already brings a peach and orange blossom note, so the fruit runs right through the glass. How the peach goes in is not printed; the bar confirms it before a server describes it.

card.front: What famous drink pairs peach with sparkling wine?
card.back: The Bellini, white peach and Prosecco. The OBX also pairs peach with bubbles, the Bigaro, plus Gentilly Gin and lemon.

components.name: Elio Perrone Bigaro
components.explain:
Bigaro is a softly sparkling pink wine from Piedmont in north-west Italy, made by the Perrone family near Asti from roughly equal parts Brachetto and Moscato. Fermented cool in tank and stopped at about 5 percent alcohol, it stays gently sweet and lightly fizzy.

Its name means mottled in the Piedmontese dialect. It smells of strawberry, raspberry, peach and rose petal.

In the OBX it tops Gentilly Gin, peach and lemon, adding fruit, a soft sweetness and a light sparkle. It is far gentler than Champagne, which is why the OBX drinks so easily in the afternoon; call it a sparkling wine, never Champagne.

card.front: What is Elio Perrone Bigaro?
card.back: A gently sweet, lightly sparkling pink wine from Piedmont, Brachetto and Moscato, about 5 percent alcohol. It tops the OBX.

components.name: Bitter orange liqueur
components.explain:
A bitter orange liqueur is a spirit sweetened and flavoured with the peel of bitter oranges, often with herbs and roots that add a pleasant bitterness. The Italian aperitivo bitters, bright orange or red, are the best-known family.

They are bittersweet rather than sweet: orange peel, gentle bitterness and a light body, made to wake the appetite before a meal.

The Chandon Garden Spritz prints a bitter orange liqueur with Chandon Brut sparkling wine and does not name it. Which liqueur, and whether the bar builds the drink or pours a ready-made spritz, are questions for the bar, so a server describes the taste rather than a brand.

card.front: Which orange liqueur is in the Chandon Garden Spritz?
card.back: The menu prints only a bitter orange liqueur, so name no brand. Describe it as bittersweet orange peel under dry bubbles; the bar confirms the rest.

components.name: Chandon Brut
components.explain:
Chandon is the California sparkling wine house founded in 1973 at Yountville in the Napa Valley by Moët et Chandon of Champagne, the first French-owned sparkling wine venture in the United States. It makes its wines in the Champagne method.

Brut means dry. Chandon Brut is crisp and fresh, with apple, citrus and a little toast.

In the Chandon Garden Spritz it is the sparkling base under a bitter orange liqueur. Because it is Californian, the menu calls it sparkling wine, never Champagne, and so does the server; the Moët link is a fair and interesting thing to tell a guest who asks.

card.front: Who founded Chandon in California?
card.back: Moët et Chandon of Champagne, in 1973 at Yountville in Napa. Chandon Brut is dry Californian sparkling wine; never call it Champagne.

components.name: Cardamom-clove syrup
components.explain:
A spiced syrup is sugar dissolved in water and simmered or steeped with whole spices. Cardamom, the green seed pod of a ginger relative, brings a cool, floral, slightly citrus perfume; clove, the dried flower bud of a tropical tree, brings warmth and a sweet, almost medicinal depth.

Both turn up in coffee traditions around the world, and clove belongs to New Orleans' flamed café brûlot.

In the Café Glacé de la Maison the syrup sweetens chicory cold brew and gives it warm spice under an orange flower foam. The guide hears an echo of café brûlot in it; how the bar makes the syrup is a question for lineup.

card.front: What do cardamom and clove bring to the Café Glacé?
card.back: Cardamom adds a cool, floral perfume and clove a warm, sweet depth, a nod to café brûlot. The syrup sweetens the chicory cold brew.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)

components.name: Orange flower water
components.explain:
Orange flower water is made by distilling the blossoms of the bitter orange tree. It is clear and intensely fragrant, used by the drop in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern pastries, and in the Ramos Gin Fizz, New Orleans' famous cream and gin drink.

It tastes of blossom rather than fruit: a heady, floral perfume that lifts cream and tea.

At Brennan's it appears twice. The Café Glacé de la Maison is topped with an orange flower foam, a floral lift over the cold brew. The Prisoner of Love prints orange flower water with gin, Earl Grey tea and clarified heavy cream. Too much tastes like soap, which is why bartenders measure it in drops.

card.front: What does orange flower water taste of?
card.back: Blossom, not fruit: a heady floral perfume distilled from bitter orange flowers. It tops the Café Glacé as a foam and scents the Prisoner of Love.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p49, eye openers, coffee and Bubbles)

components.name: Strawberry, apple and pineapple
components.explain:
The Revive juice prints three fruits. Strawberry gives colour and a sweet, red fruit perfume; apple gives body and a clean sweetness; pineapple gives tang and a tropical brightness that keeps the juice from tasting flat.

Pressed together they make a juice that is sweet but lively, fresh rather than cooked, the way cold-pressed juice is meant to taste.

The menu lists it under juices that are locally made and fresh squeezed, at breakfast and lunch. It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine, including a child, and it gives a breakfast table a bright option beside the eye openers. Who presses it is confirmed with the bar.

card.front: What fruits are in the Revive juice?
card.back: Strawberry, apple and pineapple: sweet, fruity and tangy. It is the choice for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine.

components.name: Allspice dram
components.explain:
Allspice dram, also called pimento dram, is a Jamaican liqueur made by steeping allspice berries in rum and sweetening it. Allspice is the dried berry of the pimento tree, and it tastes like clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once, which is how it got its name.

It has been traded since the 1850s, appeared in 1930s cocktail books and was taken up by the tiki bars; a little goes a long way.

In For Sentimental Reasons it sits under pear purée and sparkling wine, giving the drink its warm baking spice finish. Which allspice dram the bar pours is not printed; describe the flavour and let the bar name the bottle.

card.front: What is allspice dram?
card.back: A Jamaican liqueur of allspice berries steeped in rum, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once. It warms For Sentimental Reasons.

components.name: Pear purée
components.explain:
A fruit purée is ripe fruit blended smooth and strained, sometimes lightly sweetened. Pear purée is soft, honeyed and floral, with the gentle grain of the fruit, and it gives a drink body as well as flavour.

Purées are thicker than juice, so a purée drink feels rounder and softer in the mouth; with sparkling wine they make the Bellini family.

In For Sentimental Reasons pear purée meets allspice dram under sparkling wine, so the guest tastes ripe pear first and warm spice at the end. Whether the purée is made in house or bought in is a question for the bar.

card.front: What does pear purée add to For Sentimental Reasons?
card.back: Ripe, honeyed pear flavour and a soft body, under sparkling wine with allspice dram. Whether it is made in house is a question for the bar.

components.name: Earl Grey tea
components.explain:
Earl Grey is black tea scented with oil of bergamot, a fragrant citrus grown mostly in Calabria in southern Italy. It is named for Charles Grey, the second Earl Grey, Prime Minister from 1830 to 1834; the stories of how the blend got his name are uncertain, so tell them lightly if at all.

Bergamot gives the tea a floral, perfumed citrus note over the tannic black tea.

In the Prisoner of Love the tea joins gin, clarified heavy cream and orange flower water. The tea's acidity and tannin help the clarifying, and its bergamot meets the orange flower water, which is why the drink smells so fragrant.

card.front: What gives Earl Grey tea its perfume?
card.back: Oil of bergamot, a fragrant Italian citrus, over black tea. It scents the Prisoner of Love with gin and clarified cream.

components.name: Brennan's barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye
components.explain:
Rittenhouse Rye was introduced in 1934 by Continental Distilling of Philadelphia, named for the city's Rittenhouse Square. From 1948 it was bottled in bond, which by law means the spirit of one distilling season, aged at least four years and bottled at 100 proof. Heaven Hill bought the brand in 1993 and makes it in Bardstown, Kentucky.

It is a spicy, robust rye that holds its own in cocktails.

The menu prints Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye in Rumors are Flying. Who aged it for the house, in what cask and for how long are not printed, so a server says barrel-aged for Brennan's and no more until the bar gives the story.

card.front: What does bottled in bond mean on Rittenhouse?
card.back: One distilling season, aged at least four years, bottled at 100 proof. Ours is further barrel aged for Brennan's; the details are a question for the bar.

components.name: Tart cherry juice
components.explain:
Tart cherries are sour cherries grown for cooking and juice rather than eating fresh. Their juice is deep red, sharp and fruity, with less sugar than sweet cherry juice.

In a drink it works as both fruit and acid, so it can balance a syrup the way citrus would, while adding colour.

Brennan's uses it twice: in Rumors are Flying with barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye, brown sugar syrup and orange bitters, and in Personality with zero proof sparkling rosé and brown sugar syrup. That shared pairing is the line to sell: the same cherry and brown sugar idea, with or without spirit.

card.front: Which two drinks share tart cherry juice?
card.back: Rumors are Flying, with barrel-aged rye, and Personality, with zero proof rosé. Both add brown sugar syrup: the same idea with and without spirit.

components.name: Orange bitters
components.explain:
Orange bitters are a concentrated spirit flavoured with dried orange peel and bitter spices such as cardamom, coriander and gentian. A dash or two adds bright citrus aroma and a dry, bitter edge.

They were standard in early dry martinis and were revived in modern bars; they lift whiskey and gin drinks without adding sweetness.

In Rumors are Flying they finish the barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye, tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup, keeping the rich drink from tasting heavy and linking it to the orange peel of an Old Fashioned. Which brand the bar uses is not printed.

card.front: What do orange bitters add to Rumors are Flying?
card.back: Bright orange aroma and a dry bitter edge that keeps the rich rye, cherry and brown sugar from tasting heavy. The brand is not printed.

components.name: Daron Fine Calvados
components.explain:
Calvados is apple brandy from Normandy in northern France, distilled from cider, sometimes with some pear, and aged in oak. Pays d'Auge is its finest area, where it is double distilled.

Fine is the youngest grade, aged at least two years, so it keeps a fresh, fruity apple character with a light touch of oak. Daron Fine is a Pays d'Auge Calvados belonging to Maison Ferrand.

In To Each His Own it is the base spirit, with Lillet Blanc and quince liqueur: baked apple and perfumed quince, softened by the Lillet. For a guest who likes it, the next brandy round is the Origin Story, our Sazerac on Cognac.

card.front: What is Calvados, and what does Fine mean?
card.back: Apple brandy from Normandy, aged in oak. Fine is the youngest grade, at least two years, fresh and fruity. Daron Fine is the base of To Each His Own.

components.name: Quince liqueur
components.explain:
The quince is an old orchard fruit, a cousin of the apple and pear, golden and hard when ripe. Too sour and firm to eat raw, it is cooked into jellies and pastes such as Spanish membrillo, turning pink and intensely perfumed.

A quince liqueur steeps the fruit in spirit and sweetens it; it tastes honeyed and floral, somewhere between apple, pear and rose.

In To Each His Own it joins Daron Fine Calvados and Lillet Blanc, so apple, quince and the Lillet's orange blossom make the most seasonal drink on the fall list. Which quince liqueur the bar pours is not printed.

card.front: What does quince taste like?
card.back: Honeyed and floral, between apple, pear and rose. A quince liqueur perfumes To Each His Own with Calvados and Lillet; the brand is not printed.

components.name: Volcán reposado tequila
components.explain:
Tequila is distilled from the cooked heart of the blue Weber agave in and around Jalisco, Mexico. Reposado means rested: aged in oak for at least two months and under a year, so it keeps the agave's green, peppery character and gains vanilla, honey and soft oak.

Volcán de mi Tierra Reposado is made from highland Blue Weber agave in Jalisco and rested 135 days in American and French oak. It tastes of cooked agave, stone fruit, honey and toasted oak.

In Old Buttermilk Sky it is the base of the fall list's tequila sour, with fig liqueur, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white. It is rounder than an unaged blanco, which suits the fig and cinnamon.

card.front: What does reposado mean on a tequila?
card.back: Rested in oak for at least two months and under a year: agave plus vanilla and honey. Volcán reposado rests 135 days; it is the base of Old Buttermilk Sky.

components.name: Fig liqueur and fig syrup
components.explain:
The fig is one of the oldest cultivated fruits, soft and jammy, with honeyed flesh full of tiny seeds; figs grow well in New Orleans gardens. Dried or cooked, they taste of honey, caramel and dark fruit.

A fig liqueur is fig steeped in spirit and sweetened; a fig syrup gives the same flavour without alcohol.

The fall twins split them exactly that way. Old Buttermilk Sky uses fig liqueur with Volcán reposado tequila, and its spirit-free twin, Oh! What It Seemed to Be, uses fig syrup with Lyre's agave. Both add lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white. Which fig liqueur the bar pours is not printed.

card.front: How do the two fig drinks differ?
card.back: Old Buttermilk Sky uses fig liqueur with tequila; Oh! What It Seemed to Be uses fig syrup with Lyre's, no spirit. Both add lemon, cinnamon and egg white.

components.name: Egg white
components.explain:
Egg white has almost no flavour, but whipped in a shaker it traps air and turns a sour silky, giving it a pale, velvety cap that holds aromatic bitters or spice on its surface.

It has been used in sours and fizzes since the nineteenth century; the Ramos Gin Fizz is the famous New Orleans example. Bartenders use fresh egg white and shake it dry, without ice, before shaking with ice.

Two Brennan's drinks print egg white: Old Buttermilk Sky and its spirit-free twin, Oh! What It Seemed to Be. The guide's notes say egg white, as printed, and any question about egg goes to the service note and lineup before the server answers.

card.front: Which two drinks carry egg white, and why is it there?
card.back: Old Buttermilk Sky and Oh! What It Seemed to Be. It adds silky texture and a pale cap, not flavour; egg questions go to the service note and lineup.

items: Oh! What It Seemed to Be

components.name: Cinnamon and cinnamon syrup
components.explain:
Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of a tropical laurel tree, rolled into quills. It tastes sweet, woody and warm, the spice of baking and of fall.

In drinks it usually arrives as a syrup, sugar steeped with cinnamon sticks, because ground cinnamon will not dissolve and sits gritty on top.

Three fall drinks use it. Old Buttermilk Sky and Oh! What It Seemed to Be print cinnamon syrup with fig, lemon and egg white, so warm spice meets ripe fig. The Apple Crumble prints cinnamon with bourbon, apple cider, butterscotch and maple, the flavour of a fruit crumble. How the Apple Crumble's cinnamon goes in is not printed.

card.front: Which drinks print cinnamon, and why use a syrup?
card.back: Old Buttermilk Sky, Oh! What It Seemed to Be and the Apple Crumble. A syrup carries the flavour smoothly; ground cinnamon would sit gritty.

components.name: Cathead mandarin vodka
components.explain:
Cathead is a distillery in Jackson, Mississippi, founded in 2010 and the first distillery in the state. Among its spirits is a Satsuma mandarin flavoured vodka; the menu prints Cathead Mandarin Vodka, and that is the name to say.

A mandarin vodka carries a sweet, sunny tangerine aroma over a clean spirit; satsumas, a seedless mandarin, grow well along the Gulf Coast.

In Five Minutes More it is the base of an herbal sour with Green Chartreuse, Licor 43 and lemon: mandarin and lemon first, then the deep herbs, then a soft vanilla finish. A spirit from just up the road gives the visitor a regional story.

card.front: Where is Cathead vodka made?
card.back: In Jackson, Mississippi, at the state's first distillery, founded in 2010. Its mandarin vodka is the base of Five Minutes More.

components.name: Green Chartreuse
components.explain:
Chartreuse is a herbal liqueur made by Carthusian monks in the French Alps since 1737, from a secret recipe of 130 herbs, plants and flowers traced to a manuscript of 1605. Green Chartreuse, the stronger of the two main colours at 55 percent, is intense, herbal, minty and peppery, with a long sweet finish; the colour is natural.

It is a bartender's favourite in small amounts, the backbone of classics such as the Last Word.

In Five Minutes More it gives the deep green herbal middle between the mandarin vodka and lemon at the start and the vanilla of Licor 43 at the end. It makes the drink strong and layered, a slow sipper.

card.front: Who makes Green Chartreuse, and from how many plants?
card.back: Carthusian monks in the French Alps, since 1737, from a secret recipe of 130 herbs and plants. It is 55 percent; it gives Five Minutes More its herbal heart.

components.name: Licor 43
components.explain:
Licor 43 is a golden Spanish liqueur from Cartagena, made since 1946 from 43 ingredients, citrus, vanilla, herbs and spices, whose full list has never been published.

It tastes sweet and vanilla-led, with orange, lemon and a little cinnamon behind it; in Spain it is a favourite poured into coffee.

In Five Minutes More it rounds off the Green Chartreuse and mandarin vodka with a soft vanilla sweetness on the finish, balanced by lemon. The 1946 date is a neat coincidence for a list named for the songs of the year Brennan's opened; tell it only as coincidence.

card.front: What is Licor 43, and what does it bring?
card.back: A Spanish vanilla and citrus liqueur from Cartagena, 43 ingredients, made since 1946. It gives Five Minutes More a soft vanilla finish.

components.name: Wölffer Estate zero proof sparkling rosé
components.explain:
Wölffer Estate is a winery on Long Island, New York, known for its rosé. It was among the first American wineries to make a non-alcoholic sparkling rosé: pale salmon, dry, with strawberry, peach and citrus and fine bubbles.

The menu prints Wölffer Estate Zero Proof Sparkling Rosé, so that is the name to say. Its exact alcohol figure is read from the label at lineup before a server promises a guest zero.

In Personality it is the sparkling base, with tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup, bright and fizzy. It is the drink that lets a guest who is not drinking join the toast, and the twin of Rumors are Flying.

card.front: What is the base of Personality?
card.back: Wölffer Estate's zero proof sparkling rosé from Long Island, with tart cherry and brown sugar syrup. Read the label figure at lineup before promising zero.

components.name: Lyre's non-alcoholic agave
components.explain:
Lyre's is an Australian maker of non-alcoholic spirits, blends of natural extracts and essences in water that imitate the taste of a spirit without distilling one. Its agave is made to stand in for tequila: earthy and peppery, with a hint of citrus and smoke.

Lyre's labels its spirits under 0.5 percent alcohol, the non-alcoholic threshold, not zero.

In Oh! What It Seemed to Be it replaces the Volcán tequila of Old Buttermilk Sky, with fig syrup, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white. So a server says non-alcoholic rather than alcohol free, and reads the bottle at lineup for any guest who needs certainty.

card.front: Why do we call Lyre's non-alcoholic, not alcohol free?
card.back: Lyre's is labelled under 0.5 percent alcohol, the non-alcoholic threshold, not zero. It stands in for tequila in Oh! What It Seemed to Be.

components.name: Amarula cream liqueur
components.explain:
Amarula is a South African cream liqueur made from the fruit of the marula tree, which grows wild in the warm regions of southern Africa. The fruit is fermented and distilled, aged two years in French oak, then blended with cream; it is bottled at 17 percent.

It tastes creamy and caramel, with a fruity, slightly nutty tang. Elephants love marula fruit, which is why an elephant is on the bottle.

It is the South Africa in Floating in South Africa, poured with housemade vanilla bean ice cream and Abita root beer. Cream questions go to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What is Amarula made from?
card.back: The fruit of the African marula tree, distilled and aged, then blended with cream. It is the South Africa in Floating in South Africa.

components.name: Abita root beer
components.explain:
Abita Brewing was founded in 1986 in Abita Springs, Louisiana, across Lake Pontchartrain from New Orleans; it makes root beer as well as beer.

Abita Root Beer is made with the town's artesian spring water and Louisiana cane sugar, by a hot mix process with herbs, vanilla and yucca for its foam. It tastes like an old-fashioned soda fountain root beer, sweet, creamy and spiced, and carries no caffeine.

In Floating in South Africa it is the fizz of a grown-up root beer float, with Amarula and housemade vanilla bean ice cream. It is the same brewery as the Abita Amber in the kitchen's shells and cheese, a local link a guest enjoys.

card.front: Where does Abita root beer come from?
card.back: Abita Springs, Louisiana, made with artesian water and Louisiana cane sugar. It is the fizz in Floating in South Africa.

components.name: The float
components.explain:
A root beer float is a scoop of vanilla ice cream dropped into a glass of root beer. The cold ice cream makes the soda foam up in a creamy head, and as it melts the drink turns rich and smooth; it is an American soda fountain classic.

Classic French-style vanilla ice cream is a cooked custard of milk, cream, sugar and egg yolk, infused with vanilla and churned smooth.

Floating in South Africa is a float for grown-ups: the menu prints Amarula, housemade vanilla bean ice cream and Abita root beer. How it is built and served is not printed, so the bar confirms it. Questions about cream or ice cream go to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What happens when ice cream meets root beer?
card.back: The soda foams into a creamy head and the drink turns rich as the ice cream melts. Ours adds Amarula to Abita root beer and housemade vanilla bean ice cream.

components.name: Apple cider
components.explain:
In America apple cider usually means fresh, unfiltered apple juice, cloudy and sweet, pressed in autumn; in Britain and France cider means the fermented, alcoholic drink. The menu prints apple cider without saying which.

Fresh cider tastes of baked and fresh apple, sweet and slightly tart, and it is the base of hot spiced cider and of many fall drinks.

In the Apple Crumble it meets bourbon, butterscotch schnapps, maple, cinnamon, lemon and black walnut bitters, the flavours of a fruit crumble. Whether the cider is fresh or hard, and whether the drink is served hot or cold, are not printed, so a server describes the flavour and lets the bar describe the build.

card.front: Is the cider in the Apple Crumble fresh or hard?
card.back: The menu does not say, nor whether the drink is hot or cold. Describe the baked apple flavour and let the bar describe the build.

components.name: Butterscotch schnapps
components.explain:
Butterscotch is a sweet of brown sugar cooked with butter, rich and toffee-like. Butterscotch schnapps is a sweet liqueur flavoured to taste of it, usually low in strength and bright gold.

In American use schnapps means a sweet, flavoured liqueur, not the dry fruit brandy the word means in Germany.

In the Apple Crumble it brings the buttery, toffee note that makes the drink taste like a crumble topping, alongside bourbon, apple cider, maple, cinnamon, lemon and black walnut bitters. The lemon keeps all that sweetness bright, and the menu names no brand.

card.front: What does butterscotch schnapps bring to the Apple Crumble?
card.back: A buttery, brown sugar toffee flavour, like a crumble topping. The lemon keeps it bright; the brand is not printed.

components.name: Maple
components.explain:
Maple syrup is the sap of the sugar maple, boiled down until it thickens; about forty parts of sap make one of syrup. It comes from the forests of north-eastern North America.

It tastes of caramel, vanilla and wood, less sharply sweet than sugar, and it is a natural partner for bourbon, apple and cinnamon.

The Apple Crumble prints maple with bourbon, apple cider, butterscotch schnapps, cinnamon, lemon and black walnut bitters. Whether it is pure syrup or a maple liqueur is not printed, so a server says maple, as the menu does.

card.front: How is maple syrup made?
card.back: Sugar maple sap is boiled down, about forty parts to one, into a syrup tasting of caramel and wood. The Apple Crumble prints maple; ask the bar which form.

components.name: Black walnut bitters
components.explain:
Black walnut bitters are aromatic bitters flavoured with the American black walnut, a stronger, earthier nut than the English walnut. The best-known bottling, from Fee Brothers, tastes of toasted walnut, warm spice and molasses, with a dry, earthy finish.

A few dashes add depth and a toasty finish to whiskey drinks and after-dinner cocktails with maple, vanilla or caramel.

In the Apple Crumble they give the toasty, nutty finish under the apple, butterscotch and maple. The guide's note prints black walnut bitters, as printed; which brand the bar uses is not printed, and any question about nuts goes to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What do black walnut bitters taste of?
card.back: Toasted walnut, warm spice and molasses, dry and earthy. They give the Apple Crumble its nutty finish; nut questions go to the service note and lineup.

sources: pack service note for the Apple Crumble

components.name: Crème de banane
components.explain:
A crème liqueur is a very sweet liqueur; under European rules a crème carries at least 250 grams of sugar a litre, which gives it a thick, syrupy body. Crème here describes the texture: there is no cream in it.

Crème de banane is made by steeping bananas in spirit and sweetening it: ripe, sweet banana, sometimes with vanilla.

In Banane au Chocolat, French for banana with chocolate, it is the banana half, with crème de cacao and Pedro Ximénez sherry. It is a fine companion to the house's banana story: Bananas Foster was invented at Brennan's in 1951, so a guest who loves the Foster can sip it instead.

card.front: Does crème de banane contain cream?
card.back: The word crème means a very sweet, syrupy liqueur; there is no cream in it. It is banana steeped in spirit and sweetened, the banana in Banane au Chocolat.

components.name: Crème de cacao
components.explain:
Crème de cacao is a sweet chocolate liqueur made from cacao beans steeped or distilled in spirit and sweetened, usually bottled at 20 to 25 percent. It comes in two kinds: dark, coloured by the beans, and white, a clear distillate with a lighter chocolate flavour.

It is the chocolate in the Grasshopper and the Brandy Alexander. The menu spells it crème de cocoa.

In Banane au Chocolat it is the chocolate half, with crème de banane and Pedro Ximénez sherry, so the drink tastes of ripe banana and chocolate over dried fruit. Which brand and whether it is white or dark are not printed.

card.front: What is crème de cacao, and how does the menu spell it?
card.back: A sweet chocolate liqueur, white or dark; the menu spells it crème de cocoa. It is the chocolate in Banane au Chocolat.

components.name: Pedro Ximénez sherry
components.explain:
Pedro Ximénez, or PX, is the sweetest and darkest sherry. The grapes of that name are dried in the sun on mats until they are nearly raisins, then pressed, fortified and aged; most are grown in Montilla-Moriles and Jerez in southern Spain.

The wine is almost black and syrupy, tasting of raisin, fig, molasses and dark chocolate.

In Banane au Chocolat it gives the dried fruit depth under crème de banane and crème de cacao. The same sherry's casks finish the Rabbit Hole bourbon in the Birdcage, a small link worth knowing. Which PX the bar pours is not printed.

card.front: How is Pedro Ximénez sherry made so sweet?
card.back: The grapes are dried in the sun nearly to raisins before pressing, so the wine is dark and syrupy, tasting of raisin and fig. It deepens Banane au Chocolat.

components.name: Kahlua
components.explain:
Kahlúa is a coffee liqueur from Veracruz, Mexico, introduced in 1936 and made from rum, sugar and arabica coffee. It is sweet, dark and roasty, with vanilla and caramel.

Coffee liqueur is the backbone of the Black Russian and the White Russian, and it sweetens most espresso martinis.

In Brennan's Espresso Martini the menu prints Kahlua with chicory, vodka and Frangelico, so the coffee flavour comes partly from the liqueur. The menu prints chicory and not espresso, so how the coffee goes in is a question for the bar, and caffeine questions go there too.

card.front: What is Kahlua made from?
card.back: Rum, sugar and arabica coffee, made in Veracruz, Mexico, since 1936. It brings coffee flavour and sweetness to our Espresso Martini, beside chicory and Frangelico.

components.name: Frangelico
components.explain:
Frangelico is an Italian hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, launched in 1978 and said to recall a friar named Angelico; its bottle is shaped like a friar's habit with a rope belt. It is made with Tonda Gentile hazelnuts, the region's prized variety, with notes of coffee, cocoa and vanilla.

It tastes of toasted hazelnut and sweet vanilla.

Brennan's uses it twice on the dessert menu: in the Espresso Martini with chicory, vodka and Kahlua, and in the coffee cocktail with Nocello and whipped cream. The guide's notes print Frangelico, a hazelnut liqueur, as printed, so any nut question goes to the service note and lineup.

card.front: Which two drinks use Frangelico, and what is it?
card.back: An Italian hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, in the Espresso Martini and the coffee with Nocello. Nut questions go to the service note and lineup.

components.name: Nocello
components.explain:
Nocello is an Italian walnut liqueur made by the Toschi family company near Modena, in Emilia-Romagna, from walnuts and hazelnuts. It is amber, sweet and nutty, at 24 percent.

It belongs to the Italian walnut liqueur tradition, of which nocino, made from green walnuts, is the dark, old-fashioned cousin.

On the dessert menu it goes into hot dark roast coffee with chicory, with Frangelico and whipped cream: a roasty, nutty coffee under cool cream, gentler than the Irish Coffee because it has no whiskey and no brown sugar. The guide's notes print the two nut liqueurs, so nut questions go to the service note and lineup.

card.front: What kind of liqueur is Nocello?
card.back: An Italian walnut liqueur from near Modena, made with walnuts and hazelnuts. It goes into chicory coffee with Frangelico and whipped cream.

entries.different: The canon pours cognac with whole milk, rich syrup and vanilla extract; ours prints brandy, heavy cream and real vanilla bean, and no measures.

entries.same: Brandy shaken with cream and dusted with nutmeg: a cold, smooth, creamy drink.
entries.different: The Alexander adds crème de cacao and is served up as dessert; ours has vanilla bean and opens breakfast.

entries.label: The canon Bloody Mary
entries.same: Vodka in a seasoned tomato base, savoury and spicy, a classic morning drink; the canon is rolled, and the bar confirms ours.
entries.different: Ours adds beef bouillon to a housemade mix, making it meaty, like a spicy chilled consommé; the canon has no beef.

entries.label: Canada's savoury tomato drink

entries.different: The Caesar uses tomato and clam juice in a celery salt rim; ours uses beef bouillon and the house mix.

entries.label: The canon Sazerac
entries.same: Rye, Peychaud's bitters and an anise rinse, stirred and strained into a chilled glass with no ice.
entries.different: The canon rinses with absinthe and lists a sugar cube and lemon peel; ours names Sazerac rye and a Herbsaint rinse.

entries.different: The recipe gives measures, sugar and lemon peel; our bar confirms its own sugar, dashes and peel.

entries.label: The canon Irish Coffee
entries.same: Irish whiskey, hot coffee and brown sugar under a float of lightly whipped cream, never stirred.
entries.different: Ours uses dark roast coffee with chicory and names Tullamore D.E.W.; the canon leaves the coffee and whiskey open.

entries.label: The Table's Irish Coffee recipe
entries.same: A warmed glass, sugar dissolved in hot coffee, whiskey, then cream floated over a spoon.
entries.different: The recipe uses demerara sugar and plain coffee; ours uses brown sugar and New Orleans chicory coffee.

entries.label: Gin, lemon and Champagne
entries.same: Gin and lemon topped with Champagne: bright, citrusy and festive.
entries.different: The Flamingo adds Chopin vodka and dragonfruit and names Taittinger and Monkey 47; it is poured only in the Roost.

entries.label: The canon Old Fashioned

entries.different: The Birdcage is smoked and names Rabbit Hole Dareringer, finished in PX sherry casks, with cherry; Roost only.

entries.label: A savoury twist on the Old Fashioned
entries.same: Bourbon and Angostura in an Old Fashioned given a savoury, smoky character.
entries.different: That drink gets its savouriness from a fat-washed bourbon and maple; ours from smoke at service.

entries.label: The canon gin Martini
entries.same: Gin with a wine aperitif, cool and dry, for the martini drinker; the canon is stirred, and the bar confirms ours.
entries.different: Ours uses Hendrick's and a Corsican quinquina instead of dry vermouth, adds chive oil, and comes with caviar.

entries.label: A martini with a quinquina-style aperitif
entries.same: Gin with a French wine aperitif carrying a gentle bitterness.
entries.different: The Vesper adds vodka and Lillet; ours uses Cap Corse Mattei, chive oil and a spoon of caviar.

entries.label: The canon Sazerac
entries.same: Rye, red Creole-style bitters and an anise rinse, stirred, no ice: the Sazerac pattern.
entries.different: Ours uses stronger Willett 4-year rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters and a St. George absinthe rinse.

entries.label: The canon Sazerac
entries.same: Peychaud's bitters and an absinthe perfume in a stirred drink with no ice.
entries.different: The canon is rye; ours returns to cognac, Dudognon, with barrel-aged Peychaud's and Jade absinthe.

entries.label: New Orleans rye and cognac classic
entries.same: A New Orleans stirred drink with cognac and Peychaud's bitters, rich and spirit-forward.
entries.different: The Vieux Carré adds rye, sweet vermouth and Bénédictine over ice; ours is cognac only, served without ice.

entries.label: The canon Bloody Mary
entries.same: Vodka and a seasoned tomato base, savoury, tangy and spicy; the canon is rolled, and the bar confirms ours.
entries.different: Ours uses a housemade mix and comes with pickled okra and spicy beans; the canon has celery and lemon.

entries.label: Canada's savoury tomato drink
entries.same: Vodka in a spicy, savoury tomato base with a garnish standing in the glass.
entries.different: The Caesar adds clam and a celery salt rim; ours is tomato only, with a local pickled garnish.

entries.label: The canon Champagne Cocktail
entries.same: A bitters-soaked sugar cube under Champagne: the classic build, fizzing from the bottom up.
entries.different: Ours prints a demerara cube and names no lemon twist or cognac; the canon allows an optional cognac.

entries.label: Bitters and Champagne, Louisville style
entries.same: Champagne seasoned with aromatic bitters, built in the flute.
entries.different: The Seelbach adds bourbon, Cointreau and Peychaud's; ours is just bitters, sugar and Champagne.

entries.label: A French aperitif topped with bubbles
entries.same: A French aperitif liqueur topped with sparkling wine, light and festive.
entries.different: The Kir uses blackcurrant crème de cassis; ours uses Lillet Blanc, floral and citrus, with lemon.

entries.label: A floral sparkling aperitif
entries.same: A floral aperitif lengthened with sparkling wine: light, bright and low in strength.
entries.different: The Hugo uses elderflower, soda and mint over ice; ours is Lillet, sparkling wine and lemon.

entries.label: New Orleans cream and soda fizz
entries.same: Spirit, cream and citrus lengthened with sparkling water: creamy yet light.
entries.different: The Ramos is gin with egg white and orange flower water; ours is rum with pistachio and lime.

entries.label: Peach and sparkling wine
entries.same: Peach topped with sparkling wine: fruity, sparkling and easy.
entries.different: The Bellini is white peach and Prosecco only; ours adds Gentilly Gin, lemon and the sweet pink Bigaro.

entries.label: Gin, lemon and bubbles
entries.same: Gin and lemon topped with sparkling wine.
entries.different: The French 75 uses dry Champagne and sugar; ours adds peach and the softly sweet Bigaro.

entries.label: The canon spritz
entries.same: A bitter orange liqueur with dry sparkling wine: a bittersweet aperitivo.
entries.different: The canon names Aperol, Prosecco and soda; ours names Chandon Brut and an unnamed bitter orange liqueur.

entries.label: The Champagne house behind Chandon
entries.same: The same family name and the same traditional method of making sparkling wine.
entries.different: Moët & Chandon is Champagne from France; Chandon Brut is Californian sparkling wine, never called Champagne.

entries.label: New Orleans' flamed coffee
entries.same: New Orleans coffee, chicory-blended in local practice, served after a meal.
entries.different: Café brûlot is flamed with brandy, citrus and spice; ours is the plain hot chicory coffee, taken as the guest likes.

entries.label: A frontier way with coffee
entries.same: Strong, dark, hot coffee as a local ritual at the end of a meal.
entries.different: Cowboy coffee is boiled with the grounds in a pot; ours is a chicory blend from a New Orleans roaster.

entries.label: A café pour-over single origin
entries.same: Beans from one place, brewed to show that place, with no blend and no chicory.
entries.different: Ours is roasted in Algiers Point and rotates with the season; read today's origin from the card.

entries.label: Vietnamese iced coffee
entries.same: A sweetened dark coffee served cold, rich and roasty.
entries.different: Cà phê sữa đá drips hot coffee over condensed milk and ice; ours is chicory cold brew with spiced syrup and orange flower foam.

entries.label: New Orleans' spiced coffee
entries.same: Coffee perfumed with clove and orange, a New Orleans idea.
entries.different: Café brûlot is hot, flamed and spirited; ours is cold, spirit-free and lightly sweet.

entries.label: A spirit-free fruit classic
entries.same: A bright, sweet, spirit-free fruit drink with pineapple.
entries.different: The Cinderella mixes juices with lemon, grenadine and soda; ours is a cold-pressed strawberry, apple and pineapple juice.

entries.label: Fruit purée and sparkling wine
entries.same: Fruit purée topped with sparkling wine: soft-bodied, fruity and fizzy.
entries.different: The Bellini is white peach and Prosecco; ours is pear with allspice dram for warm spice.

entries.label: The canon clarified milk punch
entries.same: Spirit and acid clarified through curdled cream or milk and strained clear and silky.
entries.different: The canon uses milk and citrus with any spirit; ours names gin, Earl Grey and clarified heavy cream.

entries.label: New Orleans gin, cream and orange flower
entries.same: Gin, cream and orange flower water: fragrant and silky.
entries.different: The Ramos keeps its cream and egg white, foamy and topped with soda; ours clarifies the cream away.

entries.label: The canon Old Fashioned
entries.same: Whiskey with sugar and bitters: rich, spirit-forward, with orange.
entries.different: Ours uses barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye and adds tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup with orange bitters.

entries.label: The canon apple brandy cocktail
entries.same: Apple brandy as the base of a fruity, orchard-flavoured drink.
entries.different: The Jack Rose is applejack with lemon and grenadine; ours is Calvados with Lillet Blanc and quince liqueur.

entries.label: An egg white sour
entries.same: A spirit, citrus and sweetener shaken with egg white into a silky sour.
entries.different: The Pisco Sour uses pisco and lime with Angostura; ours uses reposado tequila, lemon, fig and cinnamon.

entries.label: The canon tequila sour
entries.same: Tequila balanced with citrus and a sweet liqueur.
entries.different: The Margarita is blanco tequila, lime and orange liqueur; ours is reposado with fig, cinnamon and egg white.

entries.label: A Green Chartreuse sour
entries.same: Green Chartreuse with citrus: bright, intensely herbal and strong.
entries.different: The Last Word is gin, maraschino and lime; ours is mandarin vodka, Licor 43 and lemon.

entries.ref: Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d’Alsace NV
entries.label: Our sparkling rosé by the glass
entries.same: A pink sparkling wine with red fruit and fine bubbles.
entries.different: The Pierre Sparr is a wine with alcohol; Personality uses a zero proof rosé with tart cherry and brown sugar.

entries.label: The best-known spirit-free classic
entries.same: A spirit-free, fizzy, red-fruited drink that lets anyone join a toast.
entries.different: The Shirley Temple is ginger ale and grenadine; ours is sparkling rosé with tart cherry and brown sugar.

compare.item: Oh! What It Seemed to Be

entries.label: An egg white sour
entries.same: Citrus, a sweetener and egg white shaken into a silky sour.
entries.different: Ours has no spirit: Lyre's non-alcoholic agave with fig syrup, lemon and cinnamon.

entries.label: A spirit-free canon drink
entries.same: A spirit-free drink built to taste like a real cocktail.
entries.different: The Nojito is lime, mint and soda; ours is a silky fig and egg white sour.

entries.label: A soda fountain fizz
entries.same: A creamy, fizzy, nostalgic soda fountain drink.
entries.different: The egg cream is chocolate syrup, milk and seltzer; ours is a root beer float with Amarula and vanilla bean ice cream.

entries.label: A cream liqueur dessert drink
entries.same: A sweet cream liqueur dessert drink, sometimes made with ice cream.
entries.different: The Mudslide is vodka, coffee liqueur and Irish cream; ours is Amarula, Abita root beer and ice cream.

entries.label: Spirit, cider and bitters
entries.same: A spirit with apple cider and bitters: orchard fruit and warmth.
entries.different: The Stone Fence is applejack or rye with hard cider; ours adds butterscotch, maple, cinnamon and lemon.

entries.label: The canon bourbon sour
entries.same: Bourbon balanced with lemon and a sweetener.
entries.different: Ours sweetens with butterscotch, maple and cider, adds cinnamon and black walnut bitters.

entries.label: Banana dessert cocktail
entries.same: Banana liqueur in a rich, sweet dessert drink with a dark flavour.
entries.different: The Dirty Banana blends rum, coffee liqueur, fresh banana and cream; ours is two liqueurs with Pedro Ximénez sherry.

entries.label: The Codex primer on fortified wines
entries.same: Pedro Ximénez is a fortified wine, and the primer explains how fortification and drying make it sweet.
entries.different: The primer covers sherry, port and Madeira as wines; ours uses PX as one part of a dessert cocktail.

entries.label: The canon espresso martini
entries.same: Vodka and coffee liqueur, shaken into a roasty after-dinner drink.
entries.different: The canon uses fresh espresso and syrup; ours prints chicory and Frangelico and no espresso.

entries.label: A Frangelico coffee drink
entries.same: Frangelico's hazelnut with coffee flavours after dinner.
entries.different: The Nutty Irishman is Frangelico and Irish cream; ours is vodka, Kahlua, chicory and Frangelico.

entries.label: The canon Irish Coffee
entries.same: Hot coffee with liqueur or spirit under a cap of cool cream.
entries.different: Ours has no whiskey and no brown sugar: Frangelico and Nocello in chicory coffee.

entries.label: A Frangelico coffee drink
entries.same: Frangelico's hazelnut, which can be poured into hot coffee.
entries.different: The Nutty Irishman pairs it with Irish cream; ours adds Nocello walnut and whipped cream over chicory coffee.
